Chapter 8 · 第八章

Addressing Technical Challenges应对技术挑战

— PDF p.237 —

Throughout this book, I've focused heavily on the people side of tech leadership, and for good reason. Trust, alignment, and collaboration are what make teams effective.

在本书中，我大量篇幅都在讲技术领导力中的“人”的一面，这是有充分理由的。信任、对齐与协作，才是让团队高效运转的根本。

But as a tech lead, your influence also shows up in the technical foundations your team works on every day. Architecture, deployment, testing, incident response, technical debt: these are leadership concerns too. The way you shape and evolve your systems has a direct impact on delivery speed, product quality, and team morale.

但作为技术负责人，你的影响力同样体现在团队每天赖以工作的技术底座上。架构、部署、测试、故障响应、技术债务——这些也都是领导力命题。你塑造和演进系统的方式，会直接影响交付速度、产品质量与团队士气。

This chapter is about those critical technical challenges.

本章要讲的，正是这些关键的技术挑战。

I'll start with architecture: how to lead your team through design and improvement work, whether you're building from scratch or evolving an existing system. Then I'll dive into the mechanics of modern software delivery, including integration, deployment, and testing, and how to make them smoother and more reliable. Finally, I'll tackle some common but often overlooked challenges: managing tech debt, responding to incidents, and deciding how and when to document.

我会先从架构讲起：无论你是从零搭建，还是在演进现有系统，如何带领团队完成设计与改进工作。然后我会深入现代软件交付的机制，包括集成、部署与测试，以及如何让它们更顺畅、更可靠。最后，我会处理一些常见却常被忽视的挑战：管理技术债务、响应故障事件，以及决定如何以及何时写文档。

If the rest of the book has helped you build a strong team, this chapter will help you make sure that team is set up to build strong systems.

如果本书的前半部分帮你打造了一支强大的团队，那么本章将帮你确保这支团队具备构建强大系统的能力。

Architectural Strategies and Implementation架构策略与实施

Architectural decisions shape everything a team builds, scales, and maintains. As a tech lead, you need to actively guide how your architecture looks today and how it grows and evolves over time.

架构决策决定了一个团队所构建、扩展和维护的一切。作为技术负责人，你需要主动引导架构今天的样貌，以及它随时间如何生长和演进。

— PDF p.238 —

In this section, I'll cover both ends of the spectrum, from defining a brand-new architecture from scratch to improving and evolving an existing one. You'll also learn how to make architecture more visible and actionable through clear diagrams, how to define and manage cross-functional require-ments, and how to navigate the trade-offs between innovation and stability.

在本节中，我会覆盖光谱的两端：从从零定义全新架构，到改进和演进现有架构。你还将学到如何通过清晰的图让架构更可见、更可执行，如何定义和管理跨功能需求，以及如何在创新与稳定之间权衡取舍。

Defining a System Architecture from Scratch从零定义系统架构

While most engineers work on existing systems, there are moments, like those involving greenfield projects, new products, or internal tools, where you get to define the architecture from the ground up. These are rare opportunities to shape a system intentionally from day one and set it on the right path.

虽然大多数工程师都在现有系统上工作，但总会有些时刻——比如全新项目（greenfield）、新产品或内部工具——让你有机会从零开始定义架构。这是罕见的机会，让你从第一天起就有意识地塑造系统，把它带上正轨。

Before jumping into code, take a step back with your team to answer foun-dational questions. Start with the problem: what are we solving, and why does it matter? These conversations should include product and business partners. Establishing clarity early ensures that you're designing the right thing. It also helps prevent overengineering, since you'll focus on solving a clearly defined problem.

在动手写代码之前，先和团队一起退一步，回答一些基础性问题。从问题出发：我们在解决什么问题？它为什么重要？这些对话应该拉上产品和业务伙伴一起。尽早把问题弄清楚，能确保你在设计“对的东西”。它还有助于避免过度工程，因为你会聚焦于解决一个明确定义的问题。

Once the problem is clear, examine your constraints, technical, organiza-tional, and business-related. These include decisions like which programming language to use, which cloud provider to adopt, or whether you'll follow certain internal platform standards. Make trade-offs visible. If you're optimizing for speed now, be honest about what you're deferring and plan to revisit later.

问题一旦清晰，就审视你的约束——技术上的、组织上的、业务上的。这包括诸如选用哪种编程语言、采用哪家云厂商，或者是否要遵循某些内部平台标准之类的决策。把取舍摆到台面上。如果你现在优先求快，就坦诚地说明你推迟了什么，并计划之后再回头处理。

With this context in place, begin shaping a high-level technical vision: your early hypothesis of what the system might look like as it grows. This doesn't have to be precise. A rough sketch of the major components and how they interact is enough to align the team and prompt discussion. Questions like the following will help guide you:

有了这些背景，就开始勾勒高层技术愿景：关于系统随着生长可能长成什么样的早期假设。它不需要精确。一张勾勒主要组件及其交互方式的草图，就足以让团队对齐并引发讨论。下面这类问题会帮你引导方向：

  • What are the core components or services we'll need?我们需要哪些核心组件或服务？
  • How should those components communicate or integrate?这些组件之间应如何通信或集成？
  • Are we anticipating shared infrastructure or reusable capabilities?我们是否预期会有共享基础设施或可复用能力？
— PDF p.239 —

Then shift from the abstract to the actionable. Focus on the first working version: what must exist to deliver value quickly? Zoom into that initial slice of architecture:

然后从抽象转向可执行。聚焦第一个可工作的版本：要快速交付价值，必须先有什么？把镜头推近到架构的那第一个切片：

  • What is the first component or feature to build?第一个要构建的组件或功能是什么？
  • What dependencies will it have?它会有哪些依赖？
  • What tools or technologies will we use (e.g., databases, messaging systems)?我们会使用哪些工具或技术（例如数据库、消息系统）？

You don't need detailed diagrams. Even a simple C1-level diagram from the C4 model (more on the C4 model approach in the section “Visualizing a System Architecture” on page 226) can create a shared mental model that avoids misalignment and costly rewrites later. It also makes it easier to communicate your thinking across engineering, product, and other stakeholders.

你不需要详尽的图。即便是 C4 模型里一张简单的 C1 层图（C4 模型方法详见第 226 页“可视化系统架构”一节），也能建立共享的心智模型，避免后续的不对齐和代价高昂的重写。它还能让你更容易在工程、产品及其他干系人之间传递你的思路。

As the system evolves, continue to move between the vision and the current state. Revisit your assumptions, update your diagrams, and document the deci-sions you're making. The point is to be deliberate about shifts in direction, and transparent about their implications.

随着系统演进，持续在愿景与现状之间来回切换。重新审视你的假设，更新你的图，并把你正在做的决策记录下来。关键是要有意识地对待方向上的转变，并对其影响保持透明。

It's OK if things change. They will. What matters is that the team stays aligned on what's changing, why it's changing, and what it means for the product and business. That's what a strong architectural foundation enables.

事情发生变化是正常的，而且一定会变。重要的是团队要对齐：什么在变、为什么变、对产品和业务意味着什么。这正是一个坚实的架构基础所能带来的。

Improving an Existing System Architecture改进现有系统架构

Most engineers are working within systems that already exist: codebases with history, architecture shaped by past decisions, and tech debt that comes with real-world complexity. These systems need constant improvement, and that means their architecture must evolve over time.

大多数工程师都在已有系统中工作：带着历史的代码库、由过去决策塑造的架构、以及伴随现实复杂性而来的技术债务。这些系统需要持续改进，这意味着它们的架构必须随时间演进。

As a tech lead, your role is to ensure changes happen for the right rea-sons. Resist the temptation to chase the latest trends or rewrite systems just for the sake of novelty. Start by asking questions: What real problem are we trying to solve? Are we facing performance issues? Struggling with integration? Are delivery bottlenecks slowing us down? Aligning on the true problem will help your team make better decisions, and stop you from changing everything unnecessarily.

作为技术负责人，你的职责是确保变更是出于正确的理由。抵制追逐最新潮流、或仅为新鲜而重写系统的诱惑。先提问：我们真正想解决的问题是什么？是遇到了性能问题？被集成难住了？还是交付瓶颈拖慢了我们？对齐真正的问题，能帮你的团队做出更好的决策，避免不必要地改动一切。

— PDF p.240 —

Also, keep in mind that every architecture choice comes with trade-offs. No design is perfect. Part of your role is to make those trade-offs visible, to your team and your stakeholders. Improving architecture always costs something, whether that's engineering time, focus, or added complexity. Be clear about what you expect to gain, make sure the team has the space to do the work properly, and be ready to measure whether the change actually delivers the promised value, whether that's better delivery speed, improved stability, more scalability, or reduced operational burden.

另外要记住，每个架构选择都伴随着取舍。没有完美的设计。你角色的一部分，就是把这些取舍展示给你的团队和干系人。改进架构总要付出代价——无论是工程时间、注意力，还是额外的复杂度。要清楚你期望得到什么，确保团队有空间把这件事做对，并准备好衡量这次改动是否真正兑现了承诺的价值——无论是更快的交付速度、更好的稳定性、更强的可扩展性，还是更低的运维负担。

For example, there are developers who are very keen on microservices being the best and only way to go for architecture. But who is to say that a monolith is fundamentally bad? The value of microservices comes when you need distributed ownership, when your product is scaling, or when you need independent deploy-ments to speed things up. But this doesn't mean a monolith is wrong. Actually, every startup idea usually begins as a monolith: a simple service solving a specific problem. Microservices become necessary only when scaling demands it.

举例来说，有些开发者非常热衷于微服务，认为它是架构最佳且唯一的出路。但谁又能说单体架构从根本上就是坏的呢？微服务的价值出现在：你需要分布式的所有权、你的产品正在扩张，或者你需要独立部署来加速的时候。但这并不意味着单体就是错的。事实上，每个创业想法通常都始于一个单体：一个解决特定问题的简单服务。只有当扩张需求使然时，微服务才成为必要。

Passionate, deep technical developers often get caught up in big changes: massive refactorings or endless architecture updates. I prefer to stay agnostic about specific approaches and focus on what fits the problem best. Spend more time understanding the problem and the current constraints than chasing shiny new ideas. Once you jump straight into solution mode, it's easy to lose sight of the real goal.

热情而技术深厚的开发者常常一头扎进大改动里：大规模重构或无休止的架构更新。我倾向于对具体方法保持中立，而专注于什么最适合这个问题。多花时间理解问题和当前约束，少追逐闪亮的新点子。一旦你直接跳进“解决方案模式”，就很容易看不清真正的目标。

Before jumping into any architectural change, pause and ask: What happens if we don't change this? or Why is this change necessary now? These questions help ground the conversation in real needs and avoid you falling into the “trend-driven development” trap.

在跳进任何架构变更之前，先停下来问：如果我们不改这个，会怎样？或者为什么现在必须改？这些问题能让对话扎根于真实需求，帮你避免掉进“趋势驱动开发”的陷阱。

Once there's alignment that a change is needed, don't assume it has to be all or nothing. Ask: do we really need to change everything at once? Often, a smaller incremental change is easier to execute, and easier to sell to stakeholders, than a risky big-bang rewrite.

一旦对齐了“需要变更”，不要假设它必须是全有或全无。问问：我们真的需要一次性改掉一切吗？通常，一个更小的增量改动比一次冒险的大爆炸式重写更容易执行，也更容易向干系人推销。

Here's an example from one of my teams where the big move seemed tempting but we chose a different path.

下面来自我带过的一支团队的例子：当时大动作看起来很诱人，但我们选了另一条路。

The problem问题

We had a product living inside a large monolith deployed in a datacenter. We wanted to run some quick experiments on it, but that wasn't easy. There were multiple challenges that made this difficult.

我们有一个产品，寄居在一个部署于数据中心的大型单体应用里。我们想在它上面跑一些快速实验，但并不容易。有多重挑战让这件事变得困难。

— PDF p.241 —

First, the business logic was tightly entangled with other features in the monolith, making any change risky. We couldn't confidently update one part without potentially breaking something else.

首先，业务逻辑与单体里其他功能紧耦合，任何改动都有风险。我们无法有把握地更新某一部分，而不潜在地破坏别的东西。

Second, the tech stack itself added friction: .NET with C# code, RabbitMQ, a massive MySQL database, all hosted in a datacenter. Deployments were slow and painful.

其次，技术栈本身也增加了摩擦：.NET 加 C# 代码、RabbitMQ、一个庞大的 MySQL 数据库，全部托管在数据中心。部署又慢又痛苦。

At the same time, we had a newer environment that the team used for more recent products, built on a Scala microservices architecture, running in the cloud with Kafka streams and DynamoDB. It was designed for flexibility and fast iteration.

与此同时，我们还有一个更新的环境，团队用它做更新的产品，基于 Scala 微服务架构，跑在云上，使用 Kafka streams 和 DynamoDB。它就是为灵活性和快速迭代而设计的。

The solution解决方案

It was tempting to start rewriting everything in the new stack. But there were major problems with that approach.

把一切都用新技术栈重写一遍是很诱人的。但这种做法有几个大问题。

First, it was a huge effort, impossible to estimate reliably. We could have thrown a “six months” estimate at it, but that would just have been a number with no real basis. Plus, during that time, we wouldn't be able to add any new features, which was, of course, unacceptable.

首先，这是一个巨大的工程，根本无法可靠估算。我们可以拍给它一个“六个月”的估算，但那只是一个没有真实依据的数字。而且在那段时间里，我们无法添加任何新功能——这当然是不可接受的。

Second, blindly duplicating everything meant also migrating unused features and tech debt, something that we were really trying to avoid.

其次，盲目地把一切复制过去，意味着还要迁移那些没人用的功能和技术债务——而这恰恰是我们真正想避免的。

So we asked: What's the real reason for the move? Why now? It wasn't an easy discussion, but eventually we pinned it down: we needed to improve the main ranking system, the automatic classification ranking, which was crucial for the business. In the monolith, it was very hard to experiment with changes to it. That was our real driver.

于是我们问：这次迁移的真正原因是什么？为什么是现在？这并不容易讨论，但最终我们锁定了答案：我们需要改进主排序系统——自动分类排序，它对业务至关重要。在单体里，要对它做实验性改动非常困难。那才是我们真正的驱动力。

Instead of migrating everything, we started by isolating and moving just the ranking feature. This approach is a classic example of the strangler fig pattern, a gradual migration strategy where new components are built alongside the old system, eventually replacing it piece by piece.

我们没有迁移一切，而是先把排序功能隔离出来、单独迁移。这种做法是绞杀者模式（strangler fig pattern）的经典例子：一种渐进式迁移策略，新组件在旧系统旁边构建，最终一块一块地替换掉它。

We deep-dived into how it worked. We added tests at every level. We isolated the feature from tangled logic. Unsurprisingly, we found dead code and several gaps between the actual behavior and what the product team thought it was doing.

我们深入研究了它的工作原理，在每一层都补上了测试，把这个功能从纠缠的逻辑里隔离出来。不出所料，我们发现了死代码，以及实际行为与产品团队认知之间的好几处差距。

Once we understood exactly what needed to work, we started building the new version: a fresh Scala microservice with its own DynamoDB database, con-nected through Kafka streams. After setting up the service, the ranking logic itself wasn't hard to reimplement. The real challenge was verifying it behaved identically to the old system.

一旦我们确切理解了什么必须正常工作，就开始构建新版本：一个全新的 Scala 微服务，带自己的 DynamoDB 数据库，通过 Kafka streams 连接。服务搭好之后，排序逻辑本身并不难重新实现。真正的挑战是验证它的行为与旧系统完全一致。

— PDF p.242 —

For a period, both systems ran side by side. Every night, the same data would be processed by both the old and the new system, and we compared the results to ensure perfect alignment. Once we were confident the new system matched, we cut over. All ranking requests went through the new environment, although we still updated the MySQL database in parallel, keeping the old system's dependen-cies alive.

有一段时间，两套系统并行运行。每天晚上，同一份数据会同时被旧系统和新系统处理，我们对比结果以确保完全一致。一旦有把握新系统匹配无误，我们就完成了切换。所有排序请求都走新环境，尽管我们仍然并行更新 MySQL 数据库，让旧系统的依赖继续存活。

Yes, there were downsides: increased complexity, higher operational load, duplicated infrastructure costs. But it met our main goal: we could now experi-ment fast with the ranking logic and had already started applying machine learn-ing improvements. On top of that, we now could deploy changes safely and ship in small increments.

是的，它有缺点：复杂度上升、运维负载更高、基础设施成本重复。但它达成了我们的主要目标：我们现在可以快速对排序逻辑做实验，并且已经开始应用机器学习上的改进。除此之外，我们现在可以安全地部署改动、以小步增量交付。

The takeaway经验总结

Meaningful architectural change doesn't have to be massive. Start small. Focus on solving real, current problems. Anchor decisions in clear goals, and always understand the “why” before diving into the “how.”

有意义的架构变更不必是惊天动地的。从小处着手，聚焦解决真实的、当前的问题。让决策锚定在清晰的目标上，并在一头扎进“怎么做”之前，先理解“为什么”。

Tip: If you want to dive deeper into how to design systems that support change over time, Building Evolutionary Architectures, 2nd edition, by Neal Ford, Rebecca Parsons, Patrick Kua, and Pramod Sadalage (O'Reilly) is a highly recommended resource.

提示：如果你想深入了解如何设计能够随时间容纳变化的系统，强烈推荐 Neal Ford、Rebecca Parsons、Patrick Kua 和 Pramod Sadalage 所著的《Building Evolutionary Architectures》第 2 版（O'Reilly 出版）。

Visualizing a System Architecture可视化系统架构

Before you can improve your system, you need to see it.

在你能改进系统之前，你得先看见它。

Yet many teams skip this step.

然而很多团队跳过了这一步。

I've definitely been guilty of postponing architecture visualization for too long. It's easy to get caught up in building features, fighting fires, or tackling whatever's directly in front of you. High-level work like this often slips through the cracks, especially when it's hard to explain its value to stakeholders. Until you've done the work, it's difficult to show how it will positively (or negatively) impact delivery.

我自己肯定也曾把架构可视化这件事拖得太久。人很容易一头扎在做功能、救火、或处理眼前的急事里。这种高层工作常常被遗漏，尤其是当你很难向干系人解释它的价值时。在你真正动手做之前，很难展示它会对交付产生怎样的正面（或负面）影响。

— PDF p.243 —

But if you want to make sound technical decisions, plan improvements, or add more load to your system, you need a clear view of the current state. You need to understand all the moving parts.

但如果你想做出合理的技术决策、规划改进、或给系统增加更多负载，你就需要对现状有清晰的认识。你需要理解所有运转中的部件。

My mistake was making the task too big. I'd assume I needed to review all existing diagrams, verify every system's current state, and create everything that was missing, all at once.

我的错误在于把这件事搞得太大。我会假设自己需要一次性审完所有现有图、核实每个系统的现状、并把缺失的一切都建出来。

The key is to start small. Break the work into manageable steps. Build a plan with your team to gradually develop visibility, and treat it as part of your ongoing delivery work.

关键是从小处开始。把工作拆成可管理的步骤。和团队一起制定计划，逐步建立可见性，并把它当作你持续交付工作的一部分。

First, check if there are any existing versions of architecture diagrams. Some-times you'll find bits and pieces scattered across different places that you can build on. Other times, there might already be a full diagram of the system that just needs updating. If you find one, approach it with empathy. It's easy to look at an existing system and immediately start criticizing: “How could people make these decisions?” but always keep in mind the prime directive: “The team did the best they could with the resources and time they had.” Even if it's not the best, at least you have something to start from.

首先，看看有没有现成的架构图版本。有时你会在不同地方发现一些零散片段，可以在此基础上搭建。有时可能已经有一张完整的系统图，只是需要更新。如果你找到了，请带着同理心去对待它。看着一个现有系统，人很容易立刻开始批评：“他们怎么会做这样的决定？”但请始终牢记首要准则：“团队在当时拥有的资源和时间下，已经尽了最大努力。”即使它不是最好的，至少你有了一个起点。

If there is no diagram of your current system, start building one. The sim-plest way to start is by using the C4 model approach, developed by Simon Brown, that helps you visualize systems at different levels (Figure 8-1):

如果没有你当前系统的图，就开始建一张。最简单的起点是使用 Simon Brown 提出的 C4 模型方法，它帮你在不同层级上把系统可视化（图 8-1）：

  • C1: Context — The big picture, a high-level overview.C1：上下文——全局大图，高层概览。
  • C2: Containers — Applications and data stores.C2：容器——应用与数据存储。
  • C3: Components — Internal structure of containers.C3：组件——容器的内部结构。
  • C4: Code — Class diagrams.C4：代码——类图。
— PDF p.244 —

Each level of the C4 model describes a different level of detail of a system architecture:

C4 模型的每一层，都描述了系统架构的不同细节层级：

— PDF p.245 —

C1: ContextC1：上下文

The C1 level shows the system in its environment: how your product interacts with users, external systems, and other teams. Start as simply as possible: boxes for the pieces you know, one service, one database, one entry point, and build from there. Ask your team to contribute and keep adding pieces. Every time you add a new feature or discover a new dependency, update the diagram.

C1 层展示系统所处的环境：你的产品如何与用户、外部系统和其他团队交互。尽可能简单地开始：用框标出你知道的部件——一个服务、一个数据库、一个入口点，然后从那里生长。请你的团队一起贡献，不断添加部件。每当你加了一个新功能或发现一个新依赖，就更新这张图。

C2: ContainersC2：容器

The C2 level shows the main applications and databases in your system and how they interact. Use it when your system involves multiple services or data stores. It's especially helpful for architecture reviews, planning deployments, or explaining runtime interactions and tech-stack choices.

C2 层展示你系统中的主要应用和数据库，以及它们如何交互。当你的系统涉及多个服务或数据存储时使用它。它对架构评审、规划部署、或解释运行时交互与技术栈选择尤其有帮助。

C3: ComponentsC3：组件

The C3 level shows the internal structure of a single application—its main classes, modules, or functions—and how they collaborate. Use it when refactoring, reviewing technical debt, or onboarding developers into a specific service. It's also useful when ownership is unclear or responsibilities are tangled.

C3 层展示单个应用的内部结构——它的主要类、模块或函数——以及它们如何协作。在重构、审视技术债务、或让开发者熟悉某个具体服务时使用它。当所有权不清或职责纠缠时，它也很有用。

C4: CodeC4：代码

The C4 level shows class-level design and relationships between individual classes or functions. Use it rarely, only when working in complex legacy codebases or regulated environments or when a detailed view is critical for debugging or audits. Most teams do just fine without this level. It's costly to maintain, and if your code is clean, readable, and well-structured, the added value is usually minimal.

C4 层展示类级别的设计以及各个类或函数之间的关系。很少使用它，只在复杂遗留代码库、受监管环境中工作，或详细视图对调试/审计至关重要时才用。大多数团队没有这一层也过得很好。维护它代价高昂，而如果你的代码干净、可读、结构良好，它带来的额外价值通常微乎其微。

Tip: For a deep dive into this C4 model topic, check out the C4 model website.

提示：想深入了解 C4 模型这个主题，请访问 C4 模型网站。

Start with C1, then go deeper only as needed. A good rule of thumb is to dig further when the current level of detail no longer helps you make decisions, clarify confusion, or explain the system to others. Sometimes, the C1 level might be enough to drive technical decisions internally and explain to your stakeholders the impact of their requests and why timelines may need adjusting.

从 C1 开始，只在需要时才往深处走。一个好的经验法则是：当当前的细节层级不再能帮你做决策、澄清困惑、或向他人解释系统时，再往深挖。有时，C1 层就足以在内部推动技术决策，并向你的干系人解释他们请求的影响、以及为什么时间线可能需要调整。

— PDF p.246 —

I once worked for a client migrating all their services from a datacenter to the cloud (Amazon Web Services/AWS). It was a huge company, lots of teams, and many interdependencies. My team owned a big monolith, the money maker, tightly coupled to a huge common MySQL database and many other services from other teams. We had to find a way to move this, piece by piece.

我曾为一位客户工作，他们要把所有服务从数据中心迁移到云（Amazon Web Services/AWS）。那是一家大公司，有很多团队、大量相互依赖。我的团队负责一个大型单体——公司的摇钱树——它与一个庞大的公共 MySQL 数据库以及其他团队的许多服务紧耦合。我们必须想办法一块一块地把它迁走。

This required all teams to have an overview of their services and, most importantly, their interdependencies. I remember we built this huge diagram on a Confluence page that, when zoomed out, was unreadable: lots of services, databases, Kafka streams. Someone even tried drawing it on a wall-sized board, and it still didn't fit.

这要求所有团队对自己的服务、以及最重要的它们之间的相互依赖有一个概览。我记得我们在 Confluence 页面上建了一张巨大的图，缩小之后根本没法读：满屏的服务、数据库、Kafka streams。甚至有人尝试把它画在一面墙那么大的白板上，还是画不下。

But every time we discussed a migration or someone asked how the mono-lith depended on other services, we went back to the diagram. Initially, it showed only what we knew. But with every conversation with other teams, we updated it, broadening our perspective.

但每次我们讨论迁移、或有人问这个单体如何依赖其他服务时，我们都会回到这张图。一开始，它只展示我们已知的东西。但随着与其他团队的每一次对话，我们不断更新它，拓宽了自己的视野。

While the C4 model is a great framework for visualizing architecture across different levels, it's not the only way to break things down. Another effective approach is to organize your diagrams around slices of functionality. For exam-ple, instead of one massive, unified view, you could create separate diagrams for things like checkout flow, authentication, or inventory management. Each of these can still share common components, but isolating them helps clarify purpose and reduce cognitive load.

虽然 C4 模型是在不同层级上可视化架构的绝佳框架，但它不是拆分问题的唯一方式。另一种有效的方法是围绕功能切片来组织你的图。例如，不要一张巨大的统一视图，而是为结账流程、认证、库存管理等分别建图。这些图仍然可以共享公共组件，但把它们隔离开来有助于厘清目的、降低认知负荷。

Whether you use C4, functional slices, or your own framework, what matters most is making your system visible. Once you can see it, you can evolve it.

无论你用 C4、功能切片，还是自己的框架，最重要的是让你的系统可见。一旦你能看见它，你就能演进它。

As teams increasingly adopt AI coding assistants, these tools are opening up new ways to generate helpful visualizations on the fly, without heavy up-front investment.

随着团队越来越多地采用 AI 编码助手，这些工具正开启新的方式，让你无需大量前期投入就能即时生成有用的可视化。

For example, you can use AI tools like coding assistants or chat-based interfaces to quickly generate sequence diagrams using diagram-as-code formats like Mermaid. These can be incredibly helpful when exploring an unfamiliar codebase or debugging a tricky call stack. Manually creating sequence diagrams is usually a waste of time; they're tedious and tend to go out of date quickly. But when generated quickly for one-time use, they become a powerful tool to build understanding in the moment. You don't even have to store these; just treat them as throwaway tools to help you grasp what's happening in the code more easily and move forward faster.

例如，你可以用 AI 工具（如编码助手或基于聊天的界面），用 Mermaid 这类 diagram-as-code 格式快速生成时序图。当你在探索一个不熟悉的代码库、或调试一个棘手的调用栈时，它们会非常有帮助。手动创建时序图通常是浪费时间：既繁琐又容易很快过时。但如果是为一次性使用而快速生成，它们就成了当下建立理解的有力工具。你甚至不必保存它们；把它们当作一次性工具，帮你更容易地把握代码里正在发生什么、更快地前进即可。

One particular scenario I have in mind here is a project I worked on that was built around a complex state machine. Explaining how the system worked to new joiners was always a bit of a struggle; even I had a hard time when I first joined.

我在这里想到的一个具体场景，是我曾参与的一个项目，它围绕一个复杂的状态机构建。向新加入的人解释系统如何工作总是有点费劲；就连我自己刚加入时也很吃力。

— PDF p.247 —

If I'd had an AI tool back then that could analyze the code and generate a visual diagram, showing the different states and transitions in a clear, structured way, I would've absolutely used it. It could have helped me trace how state changes flowed through the system and made those onboarding conversations far more effective.

如果当时我有一个 AI 工具，能分析代码并生成一张可视化图，以清晰、结构化的方式展示不同状态和迁移，我一定会用它。它本可以帮我追踪状态变化如何在系统中流动，让那些入职对话高效得多。

Even if these diagrams aren't 100% accurate, they can still be extremely valuable. They give you a rough map to guide exploration or uncover misunder-standings. A “good enough” diagram can often move you forward faster than no diagram at all.

即使这些图不是 100% 准确，它们仍然可能极有价值。它们给你一张粗略的地图，引导探索或揭示误解。一张“足够好”的图，往往比完全没有图更能让你快速前进。

Of course, there are limitations. If the codebase is large or you try to visual-ize the full system, the output can quickly become overwhelming or inaccurate. These tools are most effective when you focus the scope, just enough to answer the question at hand.

当然，它们也有局限。如果代码库很大、或你试图把整个系统都可视化，输出很快就会变得难以招架或不准确。当你把范围聚焦到刚好能回答当下问题时，这些工具最有效。

Just like sequence diagrams, C4 diagrams can also be generated with the help of AI tools. You can ask ChatGPT or GitHub Copilot to generate a simpli-fied C4-style representation of your architecture directly from code. For instance, you might paste in a few key files and ask, “Analyze this codebase and generate a C4 container diagram in Mermaid format. Assume it's a microservice that processes orders, with a database, an external payment provider, and a frontend client.”

与时序图一样，C4 图也可以借助 AI 工具生成。你可以让 ChatGPT 或 GitHub Copilot 直接从代码生成一份简化的 C4 风格架构表示。例如，你可以贴入几个关键文件，然后问：“分析这个代码库，用 Mermaid 格式生成一张 C4 容器图。假设它是一个处理订单的微服务，带一个数据库、一个外部支付提供商和一个前端客户端。”

These tools can offer a useful starting point, especially when working with legacy systems or unfamiliar codebases. But they're not perfect. Code rarely captures every architectural decision. Responsibilities, boundaries, and implicit contracts are often missing or ambiguous. As a result, AI-generated diagrams may be overly detailed, skip important relationships, or lack the broader context needed to interpret them effectively.

这些工具可以提供一个有用的起点，尤其是在处理遗留系统或不熟悉的代码库时。但它们并不完美。代码很少能捕捉每一个架构决策。职责、边界和隐式契约常常缺失或模糊。因此，AI 生成的图可能过于详细、跳过重要关系、或缺乏有效解读它们所需的更广上下文。

The best results come when you combine AI-generated drafts with team input. Use the AI output to trigger conversation, then refine it collaboratively. Store the final version as diagram-as-code (using tools like Structurizr DSL or C4-PlantUML) so it stays versioned, reviewable, and easy to evolve.

最好的结果来自把 AI 生成的草稿与团队输入结合起来。用 AI 的输出触发对话，然后协作地打磨它。把最终版本存为 diagram-as-code（用 Structurizr DSL 或 C4-PlantUML 这类工具），让它保持版本化、可评审、易于演进。

In the end, the point of all this isn't to produce diagrams for their own sake. These tools, whether manual or automated, are valuable only if they help you reason more clearly, communicate more effectively, and make better decisions with your team.

说到底，做这一切的目的不是为了画图而画图。这些工具——无论手动还是自动——只有在帮你更清晰地推理、更有效地沟通、与团队一起做出更好决策时，才有价值。

— PDF p.248 —

Defining and Managing Cross-Functional Requirements定义与管理跨功能需求

Cross-functional requirements (CFRs) are architectural characteristics, and they are at the heart of every system we build. They shape the structure, the behavior, and the experience of using our software, whether we notice them or not. When we talk about architectural characteristics, we're talking about things like struc-ture (the parts and how they fit together), what makes the system unique, what its purpose is, and what decisions along the way shaped it.

跨功能需求（CFR）就是架构特征，它们位于我们所构建每个系统的核心。无论我们是否注意到，它们都塑造着软件的结构、行为和使用体验。当我们谈论架构特征时，我们谈的是诸如结构（各部件及其拼装方式）、是什么让这个系统独一无二、它的目的是什么、以及一路走来哪些决策塑造了它之类的事情。

The most common CFRs you'll run into are the famous “-ilities”: accessibil-ity, compatibility, scalability, observability, reliability, and availability, but also performance and cost.

你最常遇到的 CFR，就是那些著名的“-ilities”：可访问性（accessibility）、兼容性（compatibility）、可扩展性（scalability）、可观测性（observability）、可靠性（reliability）、可用性（availability），还有性能和成本。

There are a few things these characteristics all have in common: they're nonfunctional (not directly visible to users), they're cross-cutting (impact the whole system), and they're much harder to test compared to normal functional features.

这些特征有几个共同点：它们是非功能性的（用户不能直接看到）、是横切的（影响整个系统），而且与普通功能特性相比，它们要难得多去测试。

You might have heard CFRs referred to as nonfunctional requirements, but I prefer cross-functional, as nonfunctional makes them sound like an afterthought, and that's exactly how they often get treated, until something blows up.

你可能听过 CFR 被称作非功能需求，但我更喜欢“跨功能”这个说法，因为“非功能”听起来像是事后补的——而它们往往也确实被这样对待，直到什么东西炸了。

Sometimes, the business itself makes these CFRs crystal clear. If you're working for a bank, security is nonnegotiable. It's baked into every decision, even if it slows development down. Or think of a high-frequency trading platform, where performance and speed are literally the business.

有时，业务本身会把这些 CFR 说得非常清楚。如果你在一家银行工作，安全是没得商量的。它被烙进每一个决策，即使这会拖慢开发。或者想想高频交易平台，性能和速度简直就是生意本身。

But most tech teams aren't that lucky. Most of the time, CFRs are invisible, until something breaks. Until your website loads too slowly and customers leave. Until your API falls over at 100 requests per second. Until you get hacked because security was “a later thing.”

但大多数技术团队没这么幸运。大多数时候，CFR 是隐形的，直到什么东西坏了。直到你的网站加载太慢、客户流失。直到你的 API 在每秒 100 个请求时瘫掉。直到你被黑了，因为安全是“以后再说的事”。

You already have CFRs, whether you think about them or not.

无论你是否去想，你其实已经有 CFR 了。

Every system has an expectation for speed, reliability, and resilience. The danger is assuming everyone's “common sense” matches. If you don't talk about it, you leave it open to interpretation. One person's “fast” is another's “barely acceptable.” One person's “scalable” is another's “laughably small.” That's how you get into trouble. Product says, “This feature feels slow.” You say, “It's not.” And both of you are technically right, but you weren't actually aligned.

每个系统对速度、可靠性和韧性都有期待。危险在于假设每个人的“常识”是一致的。如果你不谈论它，就把它留给了各自解读。一个人眼里的“快”，是另一个人眼里的“勉强能接受”。一个人眼里的“可扩展”，是另一个人眼里的“小得可笑”。你就是这样陷入麻烦的。产品说：“这个功能感觉慢。”你说：“不慢。”你们俩在技术上都对，但其实并没有对齐。

The earlier you define CFRs, the fewer fights and surprises you'll have down the road. Ignoring CFRs can lead to expensive and painful retrofits. Things like system performance, resilience, and observability are way harder and more expensive to deal with later. Better to make them visible and agree on them early.

你越早定义 CFR，日后的争吵和意外就越少。忽视 CFR 会导致代价高昂又痛苦的改造。系统性能、韧性、可观测性这类东西，事后处理要难得多、贵得多。最好尽早让它们可见并就此达成一致。

— PDF p.249 —

This is exactly where SLOs (service-level objectives) and SLIs (service-level indica-tors) come into play. They're just ways to make CFRs explicit and measurable.

这正是 SLO（服务等级目标）和 SLI（服务等级指标）发挥作用的地方。它们只是让 CFR 变得明确、可度量的手段。

So start defining them. You don't have to drop everything tomorrow and make a huge CFR playbook. Start small. Capture what you already have: current API response times, typical request volumes, average page loads, known security gaps. Write it down. Share it with your team. Share it with your PM. Validate assumptions. You might surface important misalignments right away.

那就开始定义它们。你不必明天就放下一切、做一份庞大的 CFR 手册。从小处开始。先记录你已经有的：当前 API 响应时间、典型请求量、平均页面加载、已知的安全缺口。写下来。分享给你的团队。分享给你的 PM。验证假设。你可能立刻就会发现重要的不对齐。

Bring CFRs into everyday conversations. When planning a new feature, ask how many users it needs to support. Add load testing to your major relea-ses. When integrating with another team's system, define what “good enough” means on both sides.

把 CFR 带进日常对话。规划新功能时，问它需要支持多少用户。在重大版本发布中加入负载测试。与另一个团队的系统集成时，双方一起定义“足够好”意味着什么。

Document whatever you find somewhere visible and versioned. Observability dashboards work great for this. If you have monitoring tools like Datadog or Gra-fana, use them to track CFRs like latency, throughput, error rates, and uptime. Where it matters most, define real SLOs and alerts. For example:

把你发现的任何东西记录在某个可见、有版本的地方。可观测性仪表盘非常适合做这件事。如果你有 Datadog 或 Grafana 这类监控工具，用它们跟踪延迟、吞吐量、错误率、正常运行时间等 CFR。在最关键的地方，定义真正的 SLO 和告警。例如：

  • SLO: 99.9% of API requests should complete in under 300 ms over a 30-day window.SLO：在 30 天窗口内，99.9% 的 API 请求应在 300 毫秒内完成。
  • Alert: Page on-call if 99th percentile latency exceeds 500 ms for more than five minutes.告警：如果第 99 百分位延迟超过 500 毫秒达五分钟以上，呼叫值班人员。

SLOs are powerful negotiation tools. They let you say, “We can't take on this new feature without risking our performance guarantees.”

SLO 是有力的谈判工具。它让你可以说：“我们不能在拿性能保证冒险的同时接下这个新功能。”

Talking about CFRs early also helps with making real trade-offs. You can't have perfect scalability, reliability, performance, security, and cost optimization all at once. Ask your stakeholders: if we had to pick, what matters most? In some cases, the choice is already made for you: depending on your industry or location, accessibility and security might be legal requirements. For a bank, it's security. For a marketing website, maybe it's accessibility. The key is to get explicit about priorities. Just saying “Everything is important” is the same as saying “Nothing is prioritized.”

尽早谈论 CFR 也有助于做出真正的取舍。你不可能同时拥有完美的可扩展性、可靠性、性能、安全性和成本优化。问你的干系人：如果必须取舍，什么最重要？在某些情况下，选择已经替你做好了：根据你的行业或所在地，可访问性和安全性可能是法律要求。对银行来说是安全。对营销网站来说，也许是可访问性。关键是把优先级明确下来。光说“一切都重要”，就等于说“什么都没有优先级”。

CFRs also help shape technical decisions. Without them, you risk overengin-eering for imaginary problems. So many startups out there plan and build for millions of users when their business plan might support only 10,000, or even fewer.

CFR 还有助于塑造技术决策。没有它们，你就有为想象中的问题过度工程的风险。外面那么多初创公司，按百万用户来规划和构建，而他们的商业计划可能只支撑一万、甚至更少用户。

Yes, business goals can change. If suddenly you do need to scale 10× faster, you'll deal with that when it happens. But it's better to adapt later than to waste months now building for problems you don't even have yet.

是的，业务目标会变。如果哪天你真的需要快 10 倍地扩展，等它发生时再应对。但与其现在浪费几个月去为你还不存在的问题而构建，不如以后再适应。

— PDF p.250 —

A very important CFR that comes with every system, and one we don't talk about enough, is cost. A simple trap teams fall into is overusing cloud resources. Cloud feels intangible: it's just so easy to spin up a new AWS EC2 machine, another database, another microservice. In the datacenter world, setting up a server meant real work, real approvals, real conversations with stakeholders. Now, it's just a couple of clicks. The easier it is to access resources, the harder they are to control. Just one more server. Just one more database. Just one more experiment.

每个系统都自带的一个非常重要、而我们谈论得远远不够的 CFR，是成本。团队容易掉进的一个简单陷阱是过度使用云资源。云感觉上是无形的：新开一台 AWS EC2 机器、再加一个数据库、再来一个微服务，实在太容易了。在数据中心的世界里，搭一台服务器意味着真正的工作、真正的审批、真正和干系人谈过。现在，只是点几下鼠标。获取资源越容易，控制资源就越难。就多一台服务器。就多一个数据库。就多一次实验。

Most teams realize the real cost too late, when the cloud bill spikes and reversing it is no longer easy. How fast you catch it often depends on the size of the company. In bigger companies, these things can go unnoticed longer. I've been there. I've had that tough conversation as a tech lead, explaining to my manager why our AWS bill was one thousand euros more because we forgot a server still running overnight after some experiments. Not easy.

大多数团队意识到真实成本时已经太晚——云账单暴涨，而要回头已经不容易。你多快能发现，往往取决于公司的规模。在大公司里，这类事情可以更久不被注意。我经历过。我作为技术负责人有过那种艰难对话，向我的经理解释为什么我们的 AWS 账单多了一千欧元——因为我们在某次实验后忘了关一台整夜还在跑的服务器。并不轻松。

The point is this: cost should always be at the back of your mind as a tech lead. Just because it's easy doesn't mean it's free. Cost is a real architectural concern, and you should treat it like one.

要点是：作为技术负责人，成本应该始终在你脑海背后。容易不等于免费。成本是一个真正的架构命题，你应该这样对待它。

Good CFR management is about making things visible early, setting shared expectations, and helping the team make better trade-offs as they build. It's about working with what you know now, being intentional with your decisions, and adjusting when new information comes in.

好的 CFR 管理，是尽早让事情可见、设定共同的期待、并在团队构建时帮他们做出更好的取舍。它是基于你现在所知来工作、有意识地做决策、并在新信息到来时调整。

In the end, thinking about CFRs early is just another way of doing the hard part of leadership: seeing around corners and protecting your team's future work from today's easy mistakes.

说到底，尽早思考 CFR，不过是在做领导力中最难的那部分：预判转角后面的东西，保护团队未来的工作不被今天的轻松错误所拖累。

Balancing Innovation and Stability平衡创新与稳定

The two extremes of innovation and stability often show up clearly in tech leads.

创新与稳定这两个极端，在技术负责人身上往往表现得很明显。

On one side, you have tech leads driven by trends, always chasing the latest tools, the newest patterns, the next big thing. They move fast, they innovate con-stantly, and sometimes they leave a trail of fires behind them. Their teams often become polyglot, using multiple programming languages and solving similar problems in different ways. Microservices multiply, each slightly different, and maintenance slowly becomes harder and harder over time.

一端，是被趋势驱动的技术负责人，总是追逐最新的工具、最新的模式、下一个大热点。他们跑得快、不断创新，有时身后留下一串火情。他们的团队常常变成多语言（polyglot）团队，使用多种编程语言、用不同方式解决相似问题。微服务成倍增加，每个都略有不同，维护随着时间慢慢变得越来越难。

On the other side, you have tech leads who stick to what they know. They push back on anything new, favoring stability and consistency. They reach for the familiar solution, even when it might not be the best fit, because it feels safer. Change makes them anxious, especially when it risks destabilizing the team or the product.

另一端，是固守自己所知的技术负责人。他们对任何新东西都推三阻四，偏爱稳定和一致。他们伸手去拿熟悉的方案，即使它未必最合适，因为那感觉更安全。变化让他们焦虑，尤其是当它有可能动摇团队或产品时。

— PDF p.251 —

Finding a balance between these two extremes isn't easy, but it's necessary, and it usually comes with experience.

在这两个极端之间找到平衡并不容易，但很有必要，而且它通常随经验而来。

My suggestion is simple: get curious about your default style as a tech lead. When you face a new technical challenge, what's your instinct?

我的建议很简单：对你作为技术负责人的默认风格保持好奇。当你面对一个新的技术挑战时，你的本能反应是什么？

Do you gravitate toward new tools and technologies, eager to try something modern, excited to bring fresh ideas into the codebase? Are you naturally drawn to innovation and exploration?

你会被新工具、新技术吸引，急于尝试现代的东西、兴奋地把新鲜想法带进代码库吗？你天生倾向创新和探索吗？

Or do you tend to lean on the tools you already know? Do you focus on stability, consistency, and making the most of what's already there? Are you naturally cautious about introducing unnecessary change?

还是你倾向于依靠已经熟悉的工具？你关注稳定、一致、充分利用已有之物吗？你天生对引入不必要的变化持谨慎态度吗？

Neither approach is inherently better. Both instincts can be valuable, and both can backfire if taken too far.

两种方式没有哪种本质上更好。两种本能都可能有价值，也都可能在走得太远时适得其反。

If you push too hard for constant innovation, you can easily overwhelm people, especially those with less experience, who need time to build depth. Your system grows more complex, as different problems get solved in different ways. Long-term maintainability suffers. And the faster you adopt new technology without a clear purpose, the easier it is to accumulate technical debt, inconsisten-cies, partial migrations, and abandoned experiments that will slow you down later.

如果你一味强推持续创新，很容易把人压垮——尤其是那些经验较少、需要时间建立深度的人。你的系统会变得更复杂，因为不同问题用不同方式解决。长期可维护性受损。而且，你越快地在没有明确目的的情况下采用新技术，就越容易积累技术债务、不一致、半成品迁移和被遗弃的实验，而这些日后会拖慢你。

If you cling too hard to stability, you can end up slowing the team's growth. You can demotivate ambitious engineers who want to learn and improve things. They'll feel blocked, and they'll leave.

如果你死死抱住稳定，最终可能拖慢团队的成长。你会让那些想学东西、想改进事物、有抱负的工程师失去动力。他们会感到被挡住，然后离开。

I know this from personal experience. I naturally lean toward stability. As a new tech lead, I always pushed my team toward consistency. Every time a team member proposed a new library or tool, I felt a knot in my stomach, because I knew I'd probably have to say no. I was afraid of losing control: over our code, over our processes, over our security.

我从亲身经历中知道这一点。我天生偏向稳定。作为一名新上任的技术负责人，我总是把团队推向一致性。每次有团队成员提议一个新库或新工具，我心里就一紧，因为我知道我大概又得说不。我害怕失去控制：对我们代码的控制、对流程的控制、对安全的控制。

But over time, I built more trust in my team. I also listened carefully to their feedback. Some of them shared, gently but clearly, that my resistance to new ideas was limiting their growth and motivation.

但随着时间推移，我对团队建立了更多信任。我也认真倾听他们的反馈。他们中有人温和而明确地告诉我：我对新想法的抵触正在限制他们的成长和动力。

So I started to change, slowly. Small experiments here and there. Nothing huge at first.

于是我开始慢慢改变。这里一个小实验、那里一个小实验。一开始都不是什么大事。

Then one day, a developer in my team proposed something bigger: running a machine learning experiment on one of our core features. He shared the idea with a few stakeholders and a few team members. Everyone was excited. I wanted to support it, but I also knew I couldn't guide him deeply through the technical side, because I didn't have enough experience myself.

然后有一天，我团队里一位开发者提出了一个更大的东西：在我们一个核心功能上跑一个机器学习实验。他和几位干系人、几位团队成员分享了这个想法。大家都很兴奋。我想支持他，但我也知道自己没法在技术层面深入指导他，因为我自己经验不够。

— PDF p.252 —

Instead, I leaned into trust. We sat down together and built a plan. We agreed he would own the project end-to-end: implementation, communication with stakeholders, tracking progress, defining success metrics. He would be the face of the project, but we would still share responsibility for how it turned out. That meant I'd stay involved, giving him visibility and support, setting up a clear, continuous check-in process between the two of us, and stepping in directly only if needed.

取而代之的是，我选择信任。我们坐在一起制定了计划。我们约定他端到端地拥有这个项目：实现、与干系人沟通、跟踪进度、定义成功指标。他会是项目的代言人，但我们仍共同承担它最终结果的责任。这意味着我会保持参与，给他可见度和支持，在我们俩之间建立一个清晰、持续的沟通机制，并且只在需要时才直接介入。

It worked better than I ever imagined. He delivered on time. The results were great. He got the rest of the team excited, started knowledge-sharing sessions, and helped upskill everyone. The product improved, and we built a reputation inside the company as an innovative, forward-thinking team.

结果比我想象的还要好。他按时交付。结果非常出色。他让团队其他人也兴奋起来，开始了知识分享会，帮助大家提升技能。产品得到了改进，我们也在公司内部树立了一个创新、有远见团队的名声。

The lesson here isn't “innovation is always good” or “stability is always bad.” The lesson is: you can expand your leadership style, one step at a time. You can find ways to experiment that feel safe, for you, for your team, for your stakeholders.

这里的教训不是“创新总是好的”或“稳定总是坏的”。教训是：你可以一步一步地拓展你的领导力风格。你可以找到让你、你的团队、你的干系人都觉得安全的实验方式。

We're seeing the impact of this balance challenge everywhere today, espe-cially with the rise of AI. Some tech teams are speeding ahead, experimenting with AI wherever they can. Others are taking a more cautious approach, con-cerned about quality and long-term implications, they prefer to carefully explore what AI can and cannot do. Both mindsets are valid, and finding the right pace for your team is key. For more on how to approach this shift in a thoughtful, sustainable way, see the section “Integrating AI into Your Team” on page 28, where I explore strategies to support your team through this transition.

今天，我们到处都能看到这种平衡挑战的影响，尤其是随着 AI 的兴起。一些技术团队一路狂奔，在一切可能的地方试验 AI。另一些团队则更谨慎，出于对质量和长期影响的担忧，他们更愿意仔细探索 AI 能做什么、不能做什么。两种心态都站得住脚，而为你的团队找到合适的节奏是关键。关于如何以深思熟虑、可持续的方式应对这一转变，参见第 28 页“把 AI 融入你的团队”一节，我在那里探讨了支持团队度过这一过渡期的策略。

Balancing innovation and stability is just another part of the everyday reality of being a tech lead, especially in a space as fast-moving as tech. The ability to continuously explore your leadership style, and adapt it not just to your preferen-ces but to your team's and company's needs, is more critical than ever.

平衡创新与稳定，只是技术负责人日常现实的又一部分，尤其在科技这样一个高速变化的领域。持续探索你的领导力风格、并不仅根据你的偏好、更根据你团队和公司的需要来调整它的能力，比以往任何时候都更关键。

There is no fully right or wrong answer. Context is everything. Environment matters. The needs of today might not be the needs of tomorrow.

不存在完全对或错的答案。上下文就是一切。环境很重要。今天的需要可能不是明天的需要。

As long as you keep checking in, with yourself, with your team, with your stakeholders, and stay open to the idea that you might also be wrong sometimes, you'll stay on the right path.

只要你持续地与自己、与团队、与干系人保持沟通，并对“自己有时也可能错”这个想法保持开放，你就会走在正确的路上。

Integration and Deployment集成与部署

Integration and deployment are two of the most critical technical processes in any product development cycle. They are the bridge between the code your team writes and the value that code delivers to your users. Smooth, reliable integration and deployment processes improve engineering efficiency and build trust across your team, your stakeholders, and your customers.

集成和部署是任何产品开发周期中最关键的两个技术过程。它们是团队写出的代码与代码交付给用户的价值之间的桥梁。顺畅、可靠的集成与部署过程会提升工程效率，并在你的团队、干系人和客户之间建立信任。

— PDF p.253 —

In this section, I'll focus on how to think about and continuously improve your CI/CD practices, define and refine your path to production, and ensure that your testing supports the speed and safety your product needs to evolve.

在本节中，我会聚焦于如何思考并持续改进你的 CI/CD 实践、定义并打磨你的上线路径，以及如何确保你的测试支撑产品演进所需的速度与安全。

Delivering Value Continuously持续交付价值

In the past couple of decades, we've seen several practices showcase how speed and reliability actually go hand in hand when delivering software. DevOps, extreme programming (XP), continuous integration (CI), and continuous deliv-ery (CD) have all demonstrated that shorter iterations tend to improve the stabil-ity of production systems.

在过去二十年里，我们看到有若干实践展示了交付软件时速度与可靠性其实是如何相辅相成的。DevOps、极限编程（XP）、持续集成（CI）和持续交付（CD）都证明了：更短的迭代往往会提升生产系统的稳定性。

Shorter iterations reduce the size of changes in each release, encourage bet-ter communication across roles, encourage a culture of automation, and enable early and continuous feedback. All of that leads to improved software stability and quality. Continuous deployment (also CD) is the natural next step in this line of thinking.

更短的迭代减小了每次发布的变更规模，促进了跨角色的更好沟通，鼓励了自动化文化，并支持早期、持续的反馈。所有这些都会带来更好的软件稳定性和质量。持续部署（也叫 CD）是这一思路的自然下一步。

Before diving in, let's clarify the terms:

在深入之前，我们先把术语厘清：

Continuous integration持续集成

Continuous integration means automatically building and testing each code change as it's integrated into the main branch. This ensures that integration issues are caught early and often, making it safer to move quickly.

持续集成意味着：每次代码变更合入主干分支时，自动构建并测试它。这确保集成问题被尽早、频繁地捕获，让快速前进更安全。

Continuous delivery持续交付

Continuous delivery builds on CI by ensuring that every change that passes automated tests is ready to be deployed to production. However, the actual deployment still requires manual approval; a person must push the final button.

持续交付在 CI 之上更进一步，确保每一个通过自动化测试的变更都已准备好部署到生产。然而，实际部署仍需人工批准；必须有人按下最后那个按钮。

Continuous deployment持续部署

Continuous deployment goes one step further: every change that passes the pipeline is automatically deployed to production without any human intervention. There's no faster way to get code running in front of your users.

持续部署再进一步：每一个通过流水线的变更，都会在没有任何人工干预的情况下自动部署到生产。没有比这更快的方式让代码跑到用户面前了。

— PDF p.254 —

Note: While the abbreviation “CD” is used for both continuous delivery and continuous deployment, the difference lies in whether the deployment step is manual (delivery) or automatic (deployment). You can absolutely do CI without CD, but not the other way around. Continuous delivery or continuous deployment can't happen without continuous integration. That's why you always see them bundled together as CI/CD.

注意：虽然缩写“CD”既用于持续交付（continuous delivery）也用于持续部署（continuous deployment），区别在于部署这一步是手动的（交付）还是自动的（部署）。你完全可以只做 CI 不做 CD，但反过来不行。没有持续集成，持续交付或持续部署都无从谈起。这就是为什么你总是看到它们被打包在一起称作 CI/CD。

I was doing continuous deployment with my team back when pushing every change directly to production still felt a little bit crazy. I thought it was awesome; I couldn't stop talking about it. In fact, my first-ever public speaking gig was about continuous deployment. That's also when I first saw the pushback firsthand. People would ask, “Only working on the master branch? Every commit going directly to production?”

我和我的团队做持续部署的时候，把每次变更直接推到生产还让人觉得有点疯狂。我觉得这棒极了；我逢人就说。事实上，我第一次公开演讲讲的就是持续部署。那也是我第一次亲眼看到抵制的声音。人们会问：“只在 master 分支上工作？每次提交都直接上生产？”

And to be fair, if you're coming from a world of long feature branches, extended phases of manual testing, and formal approval processes, then yes, code going to production within minutes can be quite the culture shock. It definitely took me some time to get comfortable with it.

公平地说，如果你来自一个长特性分支、漫长手工测试阶段和正式审批流程的世界，那么代码几分钟内上生产，确实是相当大的文化冲击。我自己也确实花了一些时间才习惯。

Even today, many teams treat CD as aspirational, something to aim for. Some are still doing fully manual deployments. And many developers are out-right against it. I think it's because they've never truly tried it, or haven't seen it done well.

即便今天，很多团队仍把 CD 当作一个愿景、一个努力方向。有些还在做完全手动的部署。而很多开发者干脆反对它。我想这是因为他们从未真正试过，或者没见过它被做好。

I get it. When I first joined Thoughtworks, I thought the idea of deploying code multiple times a day was insane. I came from an environment where we deployed once per sprint—maybe. Each release required manual approval from a manager, followed by a carefully orchestrated testing process. The idea that code could go to production automatically, minutes after being merged, felt reckless.

我懂。我刚加入 Thoughtworks 时，觉得一天部署好几次代码的想法是疯了。我来自的环境里，我们一个迭代大概才部署一次。每次发布都需要经理手动审批，然后是精心安排的测试流程。代码在合入几分钟后自动上生产这个想法，感觉太鲁莽了。

But once I experienced it done well, with proper testing, monitoring, and safety nets, there was no going back.

但一旦我经历了它被做好的样子——有恰当的测试、监控和安全网——就再也回不去了。

The thing about continuous deployment is that it's not just about tooling. It requires a fundamental shift in how the team works together. It really works only when the team collaborates effectively. It requires vulnerability, committing small changes daily, even when things aren't “done.” It requires a strong code review process, whether through pair programming or timely, thoughtful pull request reviews, alongside reliable tests and fast feedback loops. It needs a shared definition of done and clear agreement on what “ready for prod” actually means. Everyone has to be aware that a broken commit can block the whole team.

持续部署这件事，关键不在于工具。它要求团队协作方式发生根本转变。它只有在团队有效协作时才真正奏效。它需要坦诚——每天提交小的变更，即使事情还没“做完”。它需要强大的代码评审流程——无论是结对编程还是及时、认真的 pull request 评审——加上可靠的测试和快速的反馈环。它需要共享的“完成”定义，以及对“准备好上生产”到底意味着什么的清晰共识。每个人都必须意识到，一个坏掉的提交可能阻塞整个团队。

— PDF p.255 —

It demands extra care: making sure code runs locally, all tests pass, and new features are tucked safely behind flags.

它要求格外小心：确保代码在本地能跑、所有测试通过、新功能被安全地藏在特性开关后面。

Personally, I believe this is how software products should be developed and deployed. It just makes so much sense: fast feedback, no blockers, and a workflow that forces collaboration by design.

就我个人而言，我相信软件产品就应该这样开发和部署。它太合乎情理了：快速反馈、没有阻塞、以及一个在设计上就强制协作的工作流。

Now, I do acknowledge there are exceptions. Some industries, like medical or legal, might require human sign-off for every deployment due to compliance or legal constraints. In those cases, someone might literally need to push a button.

当然，我承认有例外。某些行业，比如医疗或法律，出于合规或法律约束，可能要求每次部署都有人工签字。在这些情况下，确实可能需要有人亲手按一个按钮。

Also, there are risks in implementing this approach. It's a big cultural and technical shift. Continuous deployment requires serious discipline: strong test coverage, reliable pipelines, feature flagging, and a team that treats every commit as production-ready. In complex, distributed systems, one bad change can ripple across services in unexpected ways.

另外，实施这种做法也有风险。它是一次巨大的文化和技术转变。持续部署需要严肃的纪律：强大的测试覆盖、可靠的流水线、特性开关，以及一支把每次提交都当作生产就绪的团队。在复杂的分布式系统中，一个糟糕的变更可能以意想不到的方式在各个服务间扩散。

So yes, fast delivery comes with responsibilities. And just to be clear, I'm not saying you need to embrace full continuous deployment. What I am saying is that as a tech lead, you should be aware of where the industry is heading. Con-tinuous deployment represents the current state of the art in modern software delivery. You may not need it, you may not be ready for it, but understanding its principles and trade-offs is part of growing as a technical leader.

所以，快速交付伴随着责任。我要澄清一点：我不是说你必须拥抱完整的持续部署。我是说，作为技术负责人，你应该清楚行业正走向何方。持续部署代表着现代软件交付的当前最高水平。你可能不需要它、可能还没准备好，但理解它的原则和取舍，是作为技术领导者成长的一部分。

Tip: If you're looking for a hands-on guide to implementing continuous deployment, check out Continuous Deployment by Valentina Servile (O'Reilly). It's a practical, thoughtful deep dive into the what, why, and how of modern delivery practices.

提示：如果你想找一本动手实操的持续部署实施指南，看看 Valentina Servile 写的《Continuous Deployment》（O'Reilly 出版）。它对现代交付实践的“是什么、为什么、怎么做”做了务实而深思熟虑的深入讲解。

Defining Your Path to Production定义你的上线路径

Regardless of where you are in your CI/CD journey, your code has a path to pro-duction. Sometimes it is straightforward; most times it is very messy. Whatever the state, it's your responsibility as a tech lead to ensure smooth ways of working, including your deployment process. That means making sure it's fast, smooth, and reliable and that you're continuously looking for ways to improve it.

无论你在 CI/CD 旅程中处于哪个位置，你的代码都有一条通往生产的路径。有时它很直接；大多数时候它非常混乱。无论现状如何，作为技术负责人，你有责任确保顺畅的工作方式——包括你的部署流程。这意味着确保它快速、顺畅、可靠，并且你在持续寻找改进它的方法。

But you can't improve what you don't understand. Start by gaining clarity on your current deployment pipeline: What does it look like today? What's working and what's not?

但你无法改进你不理解的东西。先弄清楚你当前的部署流水线：它今天长什么样？什么在起作用、什么没起作用？

To answer that, you need to visualize your team's path to production, a step-by-step map of how code (software change) moves from a developer's machine all the way to production. It should capture the steps, people, tools, tasks, and output involved in turning ideas into running software.

要回答这个问题，你需要把团队的上线路径可视化——一张逐步的地图，展示代码（软件变更）如何从开发者的机器一路走到生产。它应该捕捉把想法变成运行中软件所涉及的步骤、人员、工具、任务和产出。

— PDF p.256 —

I still remember the first time I had to draw my own path to production on a board and explain it to other tech leads as part of a tech lead training. I realized how many gaps I had in the process: things I was not sure about regarding how the pieces were connected and worked together.

我仍然记得第一次我不得不在白板上画出自己的上线路径、并作为一次技术负责人培训向其他技术负责人解释它。我意识到我在这个流程中有多少空白：关于各个部件如何连接、如何协同工作，我有那么多不确定。

So I brought it back to my team, and we filled in the pieces together. We even identified a couple of small changes that could reduce our time to produc-tion significantly.

于是我把它带回团队，我们一起把各个部分补全。我们甚至识别出几处小改动，可以显著缩短我们的上线时间。

I do have to mention that we were an autonomous team running on the “you build it you run it” methodology: this means we were in charge of not just developing the product but also deploying, testing, and maintaining it. There was no other infrastructure or QA team doing this for us. The company did have a vertical SRE (site reliability engineering) team, but they were managing just the very low-level underlying infrastructure and resources, like setting up the actual machines in the datacenter or setting the direction for our cloud architecture. We did have to have constant communication with them, but the rest (deployment pipelines, resource management, infrastructure cost management ) was on us.

我必须提到，我们是一支自治团队，运行在“你构建它，你运维它”（you build it you run it）的方法论上：这意味着我们不仅负责开发产品，还负责部署、测试和维护。没有别的基础设施或 QA 团队替我们做这些。公司确实有一个纵向的 SRE（站点可靠性工程）团队，但他们只管理最底层的基础设施和资源，比如在数据中心里搭实际的机器、或为我们的云架构定方向。我们确实需要和他们持续沟通，但其余部分（部署流水线、资源管理、基础设施成本管理）都在我们自己身上。

I am saying this because I know this is not the case everywhere. There are tech teams that are somewhere in the middle: where infrastructure teams play a bigger role in this process, as they define clear guidelines on how to do it, and you, as a team, have to apply them, but still build and manage your pipeline, and you have a bit more playing space with the settings and resources.

我这么说，是因为我知道情况并非到处都一样。有些技术团队处于中间位置：基础设施团队在这个流程中扮演更大的角色，他们定义如何做的清晰准则，而你作为团队必须应用这些准则，但仍然自己构建和管理你的流水线，并且在设置和资源上有一定的发挥空间。

And there are teams that completely rely on other teams, usually referred to as infrastructure teams, to deal with everything deployment-related: these infra-structure teams define the rules and enforce them. They build the deployment pipelines, and you, as a team, depend on them for any changes you might want to make in the process. This goes to the extent that some product teams don't even have access to production, just to in-between stages, and the infrastructure team is the only one that manages the production deployment.

还有一些团队完全依赖别的团队（通常叫基础设施团队）来处理所有与部署相关的事：这些基础设施团队定义规则并强制执行。他们搭建部署流水线，而你作为团队，想在流程中做任何改动都得依赖他们。这种情况甚至到了这样的地步：有些产品团队根本没有生产环境的访问权限，只能访问中间阶段，而基础设施团队是唯一管理生产部署的人。

They are all scenarios that you might fall into as a tech lead, and before deciding which one is better, remember that the particular context of the team and business and company has a lot to do with defining what is good. So, before making any rash decisions, try to understand what the current process is and why it is like that.

这些都是你作为技术负责人可能身处的情形。在判定哪种更好之前，请记住：团队、业务和公司的具体上下文，对定义“什么是好”有很大关系。所以在做任何草率决定之前，先试着理解当前流程是什么样的、以及它为什么是这样。

Here is how you can easily get started with visualizing the process.

下面是你可以轻松上手把流程可视化的方法。

— PDF p.257 —

The template shown in Table 8-1 helps you visualize your team's delivery pipeline by mapping out two key dimensions:

表 8-1 所示的模板通过勾勒两个关键维度，帮你把团队的交付流水线可视化：

X-axis (horizontal): Steps in the processX 轴（水平方向）：流程中的步骤

Each column represents a distinct step your code goes through, from the moment it's written to when it reaches users. This could include things like reviews, testing, approvals, deployments—whatever makes up your specific delivery flow. Feel free to rename or adjust steps based on your actual process.

每一列代表你的代码从被写出到抵达用户所经历的一个不同步骤。这可能包括评审、测试、审批、部署——任何构成你具体交付流的东西。你可以根据自己的实际流程随意重命名或调整步骤。

Y-axis (vertical): Key dimensions for each stepY 轴（垂直方向）：每个步骤的关键维度

Each row captures a different aspect of that step, such as:

每一行捕捉该步骤的一个不同方面，例如：

  • People involved: who's responsible or contributing here?参与人员：谁在这里负责或贡献？
  • Tools used: what systems or platforms are being used?使用工具：正在使用哪些系统或平台？
  • Tasks performed: what actions are taken?执行任务：采取了哪些动作？
  • Outcomes/outputs: what is produced or expected at this point?结果/产出：在这一步产出或期望得到什么？

Table 8-1. Path to production template / 表 8-1. 上线路径模板

Development 开发?QA 测试?Prod 生产
People involved 人员参与
Tools 工具
Tasks 任务
Outcomes/outputs 结果/产出

Note: You could consider adding an analysis column to the “path to production” template. Earlier, I described the path to production as the journey a piece of code takes from a developer's machine to the production environment. That's the typical fram-ing used by most engineering teams. But depending on your context, it might be useful to go a step further and include the pre-development stages too. Consider adding a column for analysis, the point at which a story enters planning. This is often where work starts to move and where bottlenecks can emerge: waiting on UX input, legal reviews, or decisions from other teams. Mapping these steps can help you understand delays that happen before any code is written. It's completely optional, but if your team often gets stuck early in the process, it might be worth including.

注意：你可以考虑在“上线路径”模板中加一列“分析”。前面我把上线路径描述为一段代码从开发者机器到生产环境的旅程。这是大多数工程团队采用的典型框架。但根据你的上下文，再往前走一步、把开发前阶段也包括进来可能会很有用。考虑加一列“分析”，即一个需求故事进入规划的那个节点。工作往往从这里开始流动，瓶颈也常常在这里出现：等待 UX 输入、法律评审、或其他团队的决策。把这些步骤画出来，能帮你理解在写任何代码之前发生的延迟。这完全是可选的，但如果你的团队经常在流程早期卡住，也许值得加上。

— PDF p.258 —

If you have multiple systems or tech stacks, you should have a path-to-production diagram for each. The good news is these diagrams shouldn't change too often, so once you have them, maintaining them is relatively easy.

如果你有多个系统或技术栈，就应该为每一个都画一张上线路径图。好消息是这些图不应该经常变，所以一旦你有了它们，维护起来相对容易。

The value comes from doing this as a team, with all roles involved. So make sure to bring your draft in front of your team as early as possible and fill the gaps in the process together by answering these questions together:

价值来自作为一个团队、让所有角色都参与进来做这件事。所以务必尽早把你的草稿拿到团队面前，通过一起回答下面这些问题来共同填补流程中的空白：

  • What are your dependencies?你的依赖有哪些？
  • What steps along the path to prod are still not clear to you as a team? Who can help you fill in the blanks?在上线路径上，哪些步骤作为团队你仍然不清楚？谁能帮你把空白填上？
  • In the Development column, consider the following: Who usually participates in development on this team? If you are doing pair programming, what are the pairing rules?在“开发”列，考虑以下问题：这个团队里谁通常参与开发？如果你们在做结对编程，结对规则是什么？
  • What branch strategy does the team use, trunk-based or feature branch? How is the continuous integration process of the team? Are there any rules for using Git? What happens when there are doubts about the scope of the task? And when new scenarios are discovered?团队使用什么分支策略，主干开发还是特性分支？团队的持续集成流程是怎样的？使用 Git 有什么规则吗？当对任务范围有疑问时会怎样？当发现新场景时呢？
  • In the QA column (sometimes called Sign-Off), consider the following: Who participates in this step? What happens if the story is found not to be implemented as expected? What happens if bugs are discovered during?在“QA”列（有时叫 Sign-Off），考虑以下问题：谁参与这一步？如果发现需求故事没有按预期实现会怎样？如果在过程中发现 bug 会怎样？
  • Are there any pre-production environments that need to be mapped out? Do you have dedicated environments like Dev, Staging, or QA? When are they used and by whom? Are there environment-specific checks, access rules, or blockers that impact the path to production?有没有需要画出来的预生产环境？你们有没有像 Dev、Staging、QA 这样的专用环境？它们什么时候用、谁在用？有没有环境特有的检查、访问规则、或阻碍上线路径的阻塞项？
  • In the Production column, consider this: What is the process to deploy to production? Any manual steps involved? Is there someone outside the team who participates in this? Who? What happens if the deployment is not successful?在“生产”列，考虑：部署到生产的流程是什么？有没有涉及手动步骤？有没有团队外的人参与其中？是谁？如果部署不成功会怎样？

There are endless benefits to visualizing your path to production. Here are just a few:

把上线路径可视化的好处无穷无尽。下面只列几条：

It makes your deployment process faster and smoother它让你的部署流程更快、更顺畅

Once you've built the diagram, sit down with your team and walk through it together. Ask the right questions: What are the bottlenecks in our pro-cess? Where do we have long wait times? Where does work tend to pile up? From there, identify small improvements you can start working on today. Sometimes the smallest change can have the biggest impact. For example, simply reordering tests or upgrading a library might significantly reduce waiting times.

一旦你画好了图，就和团队坐在一起把它走一遍。问对问题：我们流程中的瓶颈在哪里？哪里有很长的等待时间？工作容易在哪里堆积？从那里，识别出你今天就可以开始做的小改进。有时最小的改动能带来最大的影响。例如，仅仅重新排序测试或升级一个库，就可能显著减少等待时间。

— PDF p.259 —

In one team, there were flaky automated tests causing random failures in our deployment pipeline. Every time a test failed, someone had to inves-tigate, confirm it was a known flake, and manually restart the pipeline. Over time, this became so normalized that no one questioned it anymore. “Oh, a flaky test. Just rerun it.” It was part of our daily routine.

在一支团队里，有一些不稳定的自动化测试在我们的部署流水线中导致随机失败。每次测试失败，都得有人去调查、确认它是一个已知的偶发失败、然后手动重启流水线。久而久之，这变得如此正常化，以至于没人再质疑它。“哦，一个不稳定的测试，重跑一下就好。”这成了我们日常工作的一部分。

These tests had been around forever. No one really knew what they covered anymore, and people were hesitant to remove them, just in case they were catching something important.

这些测试已经存在很久了。没人真的还知道它们覆盖了什么，而人们又不敢删掉它们，生怕它们在捕捉什么重要的东西。

Once we started working on our path to production, identifying bot-tlenecks like this one, we also added metrics to see how often it was happening. Surprisingly, one out of five deployments was failing because of these flaky tests, way more than we thought. We decided to take action. We reviewed all the tests that were frequently failing. Some we fixed. Others we removed, accepting the trade-off that if something truly critical broke, we'd catch it elsewhere. The truth was, these flaky tests were giving us a false sense of security. People had stopped trusting them, so in prac-tice, they weren't protecting us at all; they were just slowing us down.

一旦我们开始打磨上线路径、识别像这样的瓶颈，我们还加了指标来看它发生的频率。令人惊讶的是，五次部署里就有一次因为这些不稳定测试而失败——比我们想象的多得多。我们决定采取行动。我们审查了所有频繁失败的测试。有些修好了，有些删掉了——接受这样的取舍：如果真有什么关键的东西坏了，我们会在别处抓到它。真相是，这些不稳定测试给了我们一种虚假的安全感。人们已经不再信任它们，所以实际上它们根本没有在保护我们；它们只是在拖慢我们。

Once we cleaned them up, our pipeline became more stable and more trustworthy. It was only when we mapped our path to production that the real impact became clear, and once we saw it, we couldn't ignore it anymore.

一旦我们把它们清理掉，流水线变得更稳定、更可信。只有当我们画出了上线路径，真正的影响才变得清晰；而一旦我们看见了它，就再也无法忽视。

It improves stakeholder conversations它改善了与干系人的对话

Becoming aware of your bottlenecks, delays, and improvement areas, and sharing them with stakeholders, can be a game-changer. This kind of trans-parency helps justify large estimates that depend on other teams, highlight blockers or handoffs, and build a shared understanding of why something is taking time. It also feeds into better forecasting and planning.

意识到你的瓶颈、延迟和改进点，并把它们分享给干系人，可能会改变局面。这种透明度有助于为依赖其他团队的大估算提供理由、突出阻塞或交接点，并建立对“为什么某件事需要时间”的共同理解。它还能让预测和规划做得更好。

It strengthens collaboration它加强了协作

Mapping out your path to production can bring teams closer together. On a new project, it helps define how you'll work as a team from day one. Rather than inheriting old habits or building a release process reactively, you can be intentional about the steps you take and how you collaborate.

画出上线路径可以让团队更紧密。在新项目上，它帮你从第一天起就定义你们作为团队将如何工作。与其继承旧习惯、或被动地搭建发布流程，你可以有意识地安排你采取的步骤以及你们协作的方式。

— PDF p.260 —

On an existing project, it can reveal process gaps or mismatched expectations. A shaky path to production often reflects deeper communica-tion or collaboration problems. Beyond your immediate team, these diagrams can also lead to broader improvements at the company level. When you start conversations with other teams about shared bottlenecks or dependencies, you raise visibility, and sometimes trigger momentum for cross-team process change.

在现有项目上，它可以揭示流程空白或不对齐的期待。一条 shaky 的上线路径，往往反映了更深层的沟通或协作问题。在你直接团队之外，这些图还能带来公司层面的更广泛改进。当你开始与其他团队讨论共享瓶颈或依赖时，你提升了可见度，有时还会推动跨团队流程变革的势头。

It helps with onboarding它有助于新人入职

Path-to-production visualizations make excellent onboarding tools. New joiners may not remember every step, but having a clear visual map gives them a solid overview and something to refer back to when they're unsure. I strongly believe every onboarding process should include walking through this diagram together.

上线路径可视化是极好的入职工具。新加入的人可能记不住每一步，但有一张清晰的可视化地图，就给了他们一个扎实的概览，以及在不确定时可以回看的东西。我强烈认为每个入职流程都应该包含一起走一遍这张图。

The value of visualizing your path to production is just as important even if your team does not control most of the process. A common question that comes up is “What value is there in analyzing something we don't control?” It's a fair question.

即使你的团队并不掌控流程的大部分，把上线路径可视化的价值同样重要。一个常被问到的问题是：“分析一个我们掌控不了的东西，有什么价值？”这个问题很公平。

But the most effective tech leads are the ones that are involved in all stages of development of their product, including how efficiently and reliably it makes it to production and whether it meets business expectations. Even if parts of the process are owned by other teams, understanding those black boxes, knowing who manages them, and being aware of the delays they introduce can help you work more effectively with those dependencies.

但最有效的技术负责人，是那些参与产品开发所有阶段的人——包括它多高效、多可靠地抵达生产、以及是否满足业务预期。即使流程的某些部分由其他团队拥有，理解那些黑盒、知道谁在管理它们、并意识到它们带来的延迟，也能帮你更有效地与这些依赖协作。

Take, for example, a common scenario: your deployment pipeline is man-aged by a site reliability engineering team. It might be tempting to say, “The pipeline is slow; that's their responsibility to fix.” But it's often more productive to take shared ownership.

举个常见场景为例：你的部署流水线由一个站点可靠性工程团队管理。你很可能会忍不住说：“流水线慢，那是他们的责任去修。”但更有成效的做法往往是共同担责。

In one team I worked on, our pipeline suddenly started slowing down. After about a week of waiting for it to resolve, I reached out to the SRE team to ask what was going on and whether we could help. It turned out they'd recently made a change to a config file and hadn't realized it impacted our pipeline. Once they looked into it, they discovered the issue was affecting multiple teams, but since no one had raised it, they didn't know it was a problem.

在我待过的一支团队里，我们的流水线突然开始变慢。等了大约一周也没好转之后，我联系了 SRE 团队，问发生了什么、我们能不能帮上忙。结果是他们最近改了一个配置文件，没意识到这影响到了我们的流水线。他们一查，发现这个问题影响了多个团队，但因为没人提出来，他们根本不知道这是个问题。

By stepping in, we solved our issue but also helped the SRE team uncover a broader impact. That kind of awareness and collaboration happens only when teams stay curious about the full delivery process.

通过主动介入，我们解决了自己的问题，也帮 SRE 团队发现了更广泛的影响。这种意识和协作，只有当团队对整个交付流程保持好奇时才会发生。

— PDF p.261 —

Ultimately, clarity on your path to production improves more than just delivery speed. It builds confidence, strengthens collaboration, and lays a solid foundation for consistently delivering quality work.

说到底，把上线路径弄清楚，改善的不仅是交付速度。它建立信心、加强协作，并为持续交付高质量的工作打下坚实基础。

Continuously Testing持续测试

These days, automated testing in software should come as a default requirement. The benefits are huge, and we all know it. But many of us have also felt the pain of untested code because, despite knowing better, the reality is that testing is often skipped. This is especially true in fast-moving areas like machine learning and AI, where excitement outpaces the maturity of the testing ecosystem.

如今，软件中的自动化测试应该是一个默认要求。好处是巨大的，我们都知道。但我们中很多人也尝过未测代码的痛苦——因为尽管道理都懂，现实却是测试常常被跳过。在机器学习和 AI 这样快速演进的领域尤其如此，那里的兴奋感跑在了测试生态成熟度的前面。

— PDF p.262 —

But it's not just about new tech. Legacy code, the kind that holds systems together and generates most of the revenue, is often untested too. People are afraid to touch it, and for good reason: without tests, you never know what will break. That fear paralyzes improvement, blocks features, and raises the risk of bugs and outages.

但问题不只在新技术。遗留代码——那种把系统黏合在一起、贡献大部分收入的代码——常常也是没测试的。人们不敢碰它，这很有道理：没有测试，你永远不知道会弄坏什么。这种恐惧会让改进陷入瘫痪、挡住功能、并提高 bug 和宕机的风险。

Well-done testing brings trust. It brings safety. It tells you if something's broken before it hits production. It aligns the team on what the code should do. It documents what the code actually does. It gives you a history of how features have evolved. And most importantly, it builds trust with customers through stability and reliability.

做好的测试带来信任。它带来安全。它在东西上生产之前就告诉你有没有坏。它让团队对齐代码应该做什么。它记录代码实际在做什么。它给你一份功能如何演进的历史。而最重要的是，它通过稳定性和可靠性建立起与客户的信任。

Practices like continuous integration and continuous delivery depend on proper testing to be effective. Technically, you can ship without tests, but you'll likely face more bugs, more regressions, and slower recovery. Fast tests mean fast feedback, which means faster delivery.

像持续集成和持续交付这样的实践，要有效就依赖恰当的测试。从技术上讲，你可以不带测试就发布，但你很可能面对更多 bug、更多回归、更慢的恢复。快速的测试意味着快速的反馈，也就意味着更快的交付。

A healthy testing strategy also impacts how your team collaborates. It affects pair programming, code reviews, and your ways of working. A team with no testing usually means people work in silos, and focus narrowly on getting their own code “done,” without thinking about how it fits into the bigger picture or might impact others.

一个健康的测试策略还会影响团队的协作方式。它影响结对编程、代码评审和你的工作方式。一个没有测试的团队，通常意味着人们各自为战，狭隘地专注于把自己的代码“做完”，而不考虑它如何融入大局、或可能影响别人。

I could go on about the benefits of testing, but you probably already get the point. Let's focus on why this matters to you as a tech lead. You're accountable for everything your team delivers. That doesn't just mean “it works”; it means your product meets quality standards, is scalable, and is reliable. You simply can't achieve that without proper testing.

我可以继续讲测试的好处，但你大概已经明白要点了。我们聚焦于这对你作为技术负责人为什么重要。你要为团队交付的一切负责。那不仅意味着“能跑”；它意味着你的产品达到质量标准、可扩展、可靠。没有恰当的测试，你根本做不到。

But what does “proper testing” even mean? That depends on your team. In my experience, every team is different. I've worked on projects with zero tests, some with basic unit and integration tests, and others with full-blown strategies including TDD, contract tests, end-to-end (E2E) tests, and automation across the board. There's no one-size-fits-all answer. I love TDD, but I also know context matters. Your team's environment, timeline, and maturity level all influence what makes sense.

但“恰当的测试”到底是什么意思？这取决于你的团队。以我的经验，每个团队都不一样。我做过的项目里，有零测试的，有只有基本单元测试和集成测试的，也有整套策略的——包括 TDD、契约测试、端到端（E2E）测试，以及全面的自动化。没有放之四海而皆准的答案。我热爱 TDD，但我也知道上下文很重要。你团队的环境、时间线和成熟度，都会影响什么才合理。

Start by defining what proper testing means for your team. Begin by under-standing the company-wide expectations. Are there minimum standards your team is expected to meet? Are there any tool restrictions in place that you need to respect? Once you have clarity on these aspects, assess whether your team is currently meeting them. Even if your team isn't aligned yet, as a tech lead, you need to be fully aware of these expectations because you are responsible for enforcing them.

先定义“恰当的测试”对你的团队意味着什么。从理解全公司的期待开始。你的团队有没有需要达到的最低标准？有没有你必须遵守的工具限制？一旦这些方面清楚了，评估你的团队目前是否达到了它们。即使你的团队还没对齐，作为技术负责人，你也需要完全清楚这些期待，因为你负责落实它们。

While thinking about how to measure your testing efforts, be cautious with code coverage (a software testing metric that measures the percentage of source code executed during automated testing; in simpler terms, it tells you how much of your codebase is being covered by your tests). A lot of tech teams rely on cover-age metrics to define how well their code is tested, but this can be misleading. I've seen flaky systems with 80% coverage and working systems with 20%. Code coverage doesn't tell the whole story. It doesn't account for quality, critical paths, or meaningful assertions.

在思考如何度量测试投入时，对代码覆盖率要谨慎（代码覆盖率是一个软件测试指标，衡量自动化测试期间执行到的源代码百分比；简单说，它告诉你代码库中有多少被测试覆盖到了）。很多技术团队依赖覆盖率指标来定义代码测试得有多好，但这可能有误导性。我见过 80% 覆盖率的不稳定系统，也见过 20% 覆盖率的正常工作的系统。代码覆盖率不能说明全部。它不反映质量、关键路径或有意义的断言。

If your company doesn't have clear testing guidelines, create them for your team. Sit down and build a strategy together. Start by identifying what types of testing are currently in place, whether that's contract testing, load testing, exploratory testing, or A/B testing.

如果你的公司没有清晰的测试指南，就为你的团队建一份。坐下来一起制定策略。先识别目前有哪些类型的测试——无论是契约测试、负载测试、探索式测试还是 A/B 测试。

Then, decide what testing layers you want to strengthen or introduce: unit tests, integration tests, E2E tests, and so on. Map out the tools you're already using, and note where your gaps are.

然后，决定你想加强或引入哪些测试层：单元测试、集成测试、E2E 测试等等。把你已经在用的工具画出来，并标出你的空白在哪里。

One helpful mental model to guide these decisions is the test pyramid (Figure 8-2). It emphasizes having more unit tests at the base, a moderate number of integration tests in the middle, and fewer E2E tests at the top. This structure helps balance speed, reliability, and coverage. Unit tests are fast and focused, integration tests check that components work together, and E2E tests simulate real user flows but tend to be slower and more brittle.

一个有助于指导这些决策的心智模型是测试金字塔（图 8-2）。它强调底部有更多单元测试、中间有数量适中的集成测试、顶部有较少的 E2E 测试。这种结构有助于平衡速度、可靠性和覆盖率。单元测试快速而聚焦，集成测试检查组件是否协同工作，E2E 测试模拟真实用户流程但往往更慢、更脆弱。

1 For a deeper dive, see Kent Beck's book Test-Driven Development: By Example (Addison-Wesley, 2002).

注 1：更深入的内容，见 Kent Beck 的《Test-Driven Development: By Example》（Addison-Wesley，2002）。

— PDF p.263 —

This doesn't mean blindly chasing a perfect ratio, but it's a useful principle to avoid common pitfalls, like teams that rely too heavily on slow or flaky E2E tests without having a solid base of unit or integration tests.

这并不意味着盲目追逐一个完美的比例，但它是一个有用的原则，可以避免常见的坑——比如那些过度依赖缓慢或不稳定的 E2E 测试、却没有扎实单元或集成测试底座的团队。

Finally, clarify which parts of your testing process are automated and which are still manual. Having this full picture will make it easier to spot opportunities for improvement and build a realistic, actionable plan.

最后，弄清楚你测试流程中哪些部分是自动化的、哪些仍然是手动的。拥有这张全景图，会让你更容易发现改进机会并制定一个现实、可执行的计划。

From here, shift your focus toward the biggest pain points standing in the way of better testing. Maybe tests don't run locally, and developers lose confi-dence before even pushing their changes. Maybe your CI pipeline is unstable, constantly breaking due to flaky tests that no one trusts anymore. Sometimes the tests are simply too slow, delaying feedback and slowing down your delivery process.

从这里开始，把焦点转向阻碍更好测试的最大痛点。也许测试在本地跑不起来，开发者在推送变更之前就先失去了信心。也许你的 CI 流水线不稳定，因为没人再信任的不稳定测试而频繁挂掉。有时测试就是太慢，拖慢了反馈、拖慢了交付过程。

Other times, critical parts of your system, like edge cases or infrastructure components, might not be tested at all. And in some cases, ownership of testing might be unclear or fragmented between developers, internal QA, and external QA. Each of these issues contributes to inefficiencies and risk. Document it all. Whatever you decide to improve, now or later, having a written record will help.

另一些时候，你系统的关键部分——比如边界情况或基础设施组件——可能根本没被测试。而在某些情况下，测试的所有权可能不清，或在开发者、内部 QA 和外部 QA 之间分散。这些问题每一个都会带来低效和风险。把它们都记录下来。无论你决定改进什么、现在还是以后，有一份书面记录都会有帮助。

Now that you've assessed your current state, the next step is to define what “better” looks like. This might align with broader company standards or focus on removing the day-to-day friction your team experiences. It could mean ensuring everyone can reliably run unit and integration tests locally, eliminating flaky tests that break the pipeline, or removing manual steps that delay deployments. Even small goals can lead to meaningful improvements when they're intentional and shared.

既然你已经评估了现状，下一步就是定义“更好”是什么样子。这可能对齐更广泛的公司标准，或聚焦于消除团队日常经历的摩擦。它可能意味着确保每个人都能在本地可靠地跑单元和集成测试、消除破坏流水线的不稳定测试、或移除拖慢部署的手动步骤。即使是小目标，只要是有意识且共享的，也能带来有意义的改进。

You don't need to fix everything at once. Start with the most painful, recur-ring issue that's relatively easy to address. For example, simply improving local test reliability can significantly boost team confidence and delivery speed.

你不需要一次性修好所有东西。从最痛、反复出现、又相对容易解决的问题开始。例如，仅仅提高本地测试的可靠性，就能显著提升团队信心和交付速度。

Once you've identified what to improve, work with your team to define a clear, practical strategy. Agree on your goals and how you'll get there. Whether that means introducing new practices or refining existing ones, the key is to be deliberate.

一旦你识别出要改进什么，就和团队一起制定一个清晰、务实的策略。就目标和如何达成达成一致。无论这意味着引入新实践还是打磨现有实践，关键是要有意识。

— PDF p.264 —

Whatever your vision is, define it clearly and collaboratively with your team. That shared vision becomes your testing strategy, even if the strategy is to keep things as they are, as long as that decision is intentional.

无论你的愿景是什么，都和团队一起清晰地定义它。那个共享的愿景就成了你的测试策略——即使策略是“维持现状”，只要那个决定是有意识的。

Improving testing is a business win too. When you need stakeholder support for your testing improvements, connect it to outcomes they care about: faster delivery, reduced risk, and stronger customer trust. Frame improvements in business language, not just technical jargon. Help them see that better testing will help them move faster over the long term.

改进测试也是业务上的胜利。当你需要干系人支持你的测试改进时，把它和他们关心的结果联系起来：更快的交付、更低的风险、更强的客户信任。用业务语言、而不只是技术黑话来包装改进。帮他们看到更好的测试会帮他们长期走得更快。

Once you have a clear view of your testing landscape, bring your team into the process. Collaborate on improvements. You may even be able to delegate ownership to someone interested in driving this forward, organizing team ses-sions, documenting the current state, and helping prioritize fixes. Remember: being accountable doesn't mean doing everything yourself.

一旦你对测试全貌有了清晰认识，就把团队拉进流程。协作改进。你甚至可以把所有权委托给有兴趣推动这件事的人——组织团队会议、记录现状、帮忙给修复排优先级。记住：担责不意味着什么都自己做。

Even when you delegate, your role as a tech lead remains critical. You do need to think deliberately about what testing should look like for your team. Stay close to the process. Even if a separate QA team handles much of the work, make sure you understand how testing impacts your timelines, your risks, and your delivery flow. Work closely with this other team. Stay alert to bottlenecks and blind spots.

即使你委托出去，你作为技术负责人的角色仍然关键。你确实需要有意识地思考你的团队的测试应该是什么样子。贴近流程。即使一个独立的 QA 团队处理大部分工作，也要确保你理解测试如何影响你的时间线、你的风险和你的交付流。与那个团队紧密合作。对瓶颈和盲点保持警觉。

Testing is one of the fundamental practices that underpins everything else we do as tech leads. It connects to how we manage risk, improve delivery speed, and build trust, both within our teams and with our stakeholders.

测试是支撑我们作为技术负责人所做一切的基础实践之一。它连接着我们如何管理风险、提升交付速度、以及在团队内部和与干系人之间建立信任。

Common Technical Challenges and How to Overcome Them常见技术挑战及应对方法

Every tech team deals with messy, unglamorous problems. The kind that don't get talked about in architecture diagrams or sprint demos, but they slow you down, frustrate your team, and get in the way of delivering value. As a tech lead, you're expected to navigate these challenges and help your team do the same.

每个技术团队都在处理那些乱糟糟、不光鲜的问题。那种不会出现在架构图或迭代演示里的问题，但它们拖慢你、让团队沮丧、挡住你交付价值的路。作为技术负责人，你被期望驾驭这些挑战，并帮你的团队也做到。
