This section is about those common technical struggles that every team faces at some point: growing tech debt that never makes it into the roadmap, incidents that catch you off guard and leave everyone scrambling, and the constant ques-tion of how much documentation is enough.

本节要讲的，是每个团队在某个时刻都会面对的那些常见技术挣扎：永远进不了路线图的不断增长的技术债务、把你打个措手不及、让所有人手忙脚乱的故障事件，以及“文档到底写多少才够”这个永恒的问题。

I'll go through each of these with practical strategies you can use to tackle them—not perfectly but better. Because handling these well is what separates a team that survives from one that thrives.

我会逐一讲这些，并给出你可以用来应对它们的实用策略——不是完美地，而是更好地。因为把这些处理好，正是区分一支“存活下来的团队”和一支“茁壮成长的团队”的关键。

— PDF p.265 —

Managing Technical Debt管理技术债务

The only project without tech debt is the one that hasn't started.

唯一没有技术债务的项目，是还没开始的那个项目。

Tech debt is part of building software; it's unavoidable. In fact, in my expe-rience, the most successful, revenue-driving systems are often the ones that happen to accumulate the most tech debt. Why? Because they've grown fast to meet demand. Because they're actively used. And because there's no way to build a real-world product at speed without making some compromises along the way.

技术债务是构建软件的一部分；它不可避免。事实上，以我的经验，最成功、最创收的系统，往往偏偏是积累技术债务最多的那些。为什么？因为它们为满足需求而快速增长。因为它们被积极地使用。因为要快速构建一个真实世界的产品，一路上不可能不做一些妥协。

Sometimes, tech debt is intentional: you cut corners to move quickly. Maybe you duplicate code, couple components too tightly, or skip testing. You promise yourself you'll fix it later, when there's more time…but “later” rarely comes, as it's not properly prioritized. There's always another feature, another deadline that comes first.

有时，技术债务是有意为之的：你为了快走而抄了近道。也许你复制了代码、把组件耦合得太紧、或跳过了测试。你向自己承诺以后时间多了再修……但“以后”很少到来，因为它没有被妥善排优先级。总是有另一个功能、另一个截止日期排在前面。

Other times, debt creeps in even when you don't touch the code. Third-party libraries move forward, while your system stays still. Over time, what once worked fine becomes outdated, buggy, or even insecure.

另一些时候，即使你没碰代码，债务也会悄悄溜进来。第三方库在前进，而你的系统原地不动。随着时间推移，曾经好好的东西变得过时、有 bug、甚至不安全。

And tech debt isn't just in the code. There's also product tech debt: all those old features nobody uses, built in hacky ways that no one fully understands anymore. I've seen this kind of debt slow teams down more than any messy codebase, because new work must still integrate with and tiptoe around those unknowns.

而且技术债务不只在代码里。还有产品技术债务：那些没人用的老功能，以没人完全理解的 hacky 方式构建。我见过这种债务比任何凌乱代码库都更拖团队的后腿，因为新工作仍然必须与那些未知物集成、并小心翼翼地绕着它们走。

So no, you can't avoid tech debt. But you do need to manage it.

所以，你无法避免技术债务。但你确实需要管理它。

If you ignore it, it grows into a bottleneck. Every new feature takes longer. Outages become more frequent. Engineers grow frustrated and disengaged.

如果你忽视它，它会长成一个瓶颈。每个新功能都要花更久。宕机变得更频繁。工程师变得沮丧、失去投入。

Beyond the technical consequences, unmanaged tech debt chips away at morale. When your team is constantly tripping over fragile systems and patching problems they didn't create, it wears them down. It becomes harder to feel proud of the work. And over time, that erodes retention and team health.

除了技术后果，未管理的技术债务还会一点点侵蚀士气。当你的团队不断被脆弱的系统绊倒、修补不是他们造成的问题时，这会把他们磨垮。为工作感到自豪变得越来越难。而随着时间推移，这会侵蚀留任率和团队健康。

Fortunately, there are ways to keep tech debt from spiraling. The first step is making it visible. You can't manage what you can't see.

幸运的是，有办法防止技术债务失控。第一步是让它可见。你无法管理你看不见的东西。

Start by identifying and listing all known tech debt items across your system. This process alone gives clarity on the scale and impact, and it helps frame future conversations with your team and stakeholders.

先识别并列出你系统中所有已知的技术债务项。仅这个过程就能让你看清规模和影响，并帮你框定未来与团队和干系人的对话。

One practical way to do this is to create a “Tech Debt Wall.” This could be a shared Confluence page, a board in Jira, or even a physical space in the office. The idea is to make the most pressing tech debt items visible and transparent to the entire team and relevant stakeholders. You can include context, impact, and links to related issues or documentation. This helps prioritize discussions and reinforces that tech debt is an ongoing part of your product's health.

一个实用的做法是建一面“技术债务墙”。它可以是一个共享的 Confluence 页面、Jira 里的一个看板、甚至办公室里的一面物理墙。思路是把最紧迫的技术债务项对整个团队和相关干系人变得可见、透明。你可以附上上下文、影响、以及指向相关问题或文档的链接。这有助于给讨论排优先级，并强化“技术债务是你产品健康中持续存在的一部分”这个认知。

— PDF p.266 —

Another effective method is using an effort-value matrix. This is a collabora-tive tool where your team evaluates each piece of technical debt by plotting it on a 2 × 2 grid, with “effort to resolve” on one axis and “value of resolving” on the other.

另一个有效的方法是使用“投入—价值矩阵”。这是一个协作工具，你的团队把每一项技术债务画在一个 2×2 网格上进行评估：一个轴是“解决所需投入”，另一个轴是“解决带来的价值”。

The goal is to move away from gut feelings and create a shared, visual representation of priorities. It helps uncover hidden quick wins (high value, low effort) and align team discussions around what really matters.

目标是跳出凭感觉行事，建立一个共享的、可视化的优先级表示。它帮你发现隐藏的速赢（高价值、低投入），并让团队的讨论围绕真正重要的事对齐。

Plus, it's a great way to include product managers in the decision-making process, since it translates technical trade-offs into clear business value. Tasks in the top-left quadrant in Figure 8-3 (high value, low effort) are your low-hanging fruit and a great way to start.

此外，它是让产品经理参与决策过程的好方法，因为它把技术取舍翻译成清晰的业务价值。图 8-3 左上象限里的任务（高价值、低投入）是你垂手可得的果实，也是一个很好的起点。

In addition to the effort-value matrix, you can use more nuanced prioritiza-tion frameworks that take into account not just effort and value but also risk, frequency of impact, and alignment with strategic goals. For example, assigning scores to each of these dimensions, on a 1–5 scale, can help you generate a composite priority score. This makes trade-offs easier to justify and decisions more transparent when discussing priorities with stakeholders or leadership. Tools like RICE (reach, impact, confidence, effort) or custom-weighted models can be adapted for this purpose.

除了投入—价值矩阵，你还可以使用更细致的优先级框架，不仅考虑投入和价值，还考虑风险、影响频率以及与战略目标的一致性。例如，给这些维度的每一项按 1–5 分打分，可以帮你生成一个综合优先级分数。这让取舍更容易被证明、让决策在与干系人或领导层讨论优先级时更透明。像 RICE（触达范围 reach、影响 impact、信心 confidence、投入 effort）或自定义加权模型这样的工具，都可以为此改造使用。

— PDF p.267 —

Use whatever framework fits your team's decision-making style, but the key is to move from opinion to evidence-based prioritization. Start somewhere. Prioritize the tasks. Add them to your backlog. Work with product people in your team to build a strategy around them.

用任何适合你团队决策风格的框架，但关键是从“凭观点”走向“基于证据的优先级排序”。从某个地方开始。给任务排优先级。把它们加进你的待办列表。和团队里的产品同事一起围绕它们制定策略。

Now that you have them prioritized, here are some strategies for how you can start introducing these tasks in your daily team work:

既然你已经排好了优先级，下面是一些策略，教你如何把这些任务引入团队日常工作：

The 80/20 rule80/20 法则

Reserve 20% of your team's capacity each sprint to reduce tech debt.

每个迭代预留团队 20% 的产能来偿还技术债务。

Package tech debt work alongside relevant product initiatives把技术债务工作与相关产品 initiative 打包在一起

For example, if you're touching a part of the codebase to build a new feature, use that moment to clean up related debt in the same area.

例如，如果你为了做一个新功能而正在改某部分代码库，就借着那个时机把同一区域的相关债务清理掉。

Theme-based sprints主题式迭代

Focus each cycle on a particular type of technical debt, such as performance optimizations, test coverage, or security hardening. This helps the team dive deeper into a specific area.

每个周期聚焦一类特定的技术债务，比如性能优化、测试覆盖或安全加固。这帮团队更深入地钻进某个具体领域。

Definition of done完成定义

Expand your DoD (definition of done) to include debt-related criteria (e.g., no new dependencies added without review).

扩展你的 DoD（完成定义），把债务相关标准包括进去（例如：未经评审不得引入新依赖）。

In addition to visualization exercises, consider using tools that help you track and monitor technical debt over time. Platforms like Code Climate, SonarQube, and Stepsize that integrate directly into your codebase and CI pipeline, highlight-ing hotspots, code complexity, and maintainability issues.

除了可视化练习，考虑使用帮你随时间跟踪和监控技术债务的工具。像 Code Climate、SonarQube 和 Stepsize 这样的平台，直接集成到你的代码库和 CI 流水线中，高亮热点、代码复杂度和可维护性问题。

For backlog-level management, tools like Jira, Asana, or Linear can be struc-tured to tag and group technical debt items by type, impact, or urgency. The key is to choose tools your team will actually use and keep them tightly integrated into your workflows.

对待办列表级别的管理，像 Jira、Asana 或 Linear 这样的工具可以被组织起来，按类型、影响或紧急程度给技术债务项打标签、分组。关键是选择你的团队真正会用的工具，并让它们紧密集成到你的工作流中。

This sounds like a lot, but again, I have to remind you that as a tech lead, you need to ensure tech debt is taken care of. It's actually a great opportunity to delegate. In my team, we had a rotating role called the Tech Debt Champion.

这听起来很多，但我还是要提醒你：作为技术负责人，你需要确保技术债务被照料好。这其实是一个绝佳的委托机会。在我的团队里，我们有一个轮换的角色，叫“技术债务代言人”（Tech Debt Champion）。

— PDF p.268 —

This person's focus was to keep the list up-to-date, gather input from engineers, and surface the most painful areas of the codebase. You can even rotate this role, giving multiple people the chance to develop extra skills. You just have to ensure this person is properly set up for success to deal with the task. For a detailed plan on how to delegate effectively, check out Chapter 6.

这个人的职责是保持清单更新、收集工程师的意见、并浮现代码库中最痛的区域。你甚至可以轮换这个角色，让多个人有机会发展额外技能。你只需要确保这个人被妥善地赋予成功应对这项任务的条件。关于如何有效委托的详细计划，见第 6 章。

When defining success metrics, avoid goals like “eliminate all tech debt.” That's not realistic, or even necessary. Some tech debt is totally tolerable. In my team, we explicitly acknowledged certain debt we would live with, because we understood the trade-offs and risks. The key is intentionality: manage it deliber-ately, know why it's there, and make sure it doesn't silently grow into something harmful. The goal is sustainable control.

定义成功指标时，避免“消除所有技术债务”这样的目标。那不现实，甚至没必要。有些技术债务是完全可以容忍的。在我的团队里，我们明确承认某些我们愿意与之共存的债务，因为我们理解其中的取舍和风险。关键是有意识：审慎地管理它、知道它为什么在那里、并确保它不会悄悄长成有害的东西。目标是可持续的控制。

Tech debt is not the enemy. Poorly managed tech debt is. Done right, tech debt can actually be strategic. It lets you ship faster, validate ideas quickly, and seize market opportunities.

技术债务不是敌人。管理糟糕的技术债务才是。处理得当，技术债务实际上可以是战略性的。它让你交付更快、快速验证想法、抓住市场机会。

The next challenge is selling tech debt work to your stakeholders.

下一个挑战是向你的干系人推销技术债务工作。

Let's say you've identified a few areas of tech debt that are slowing your team down. Maybe your CI pipeline is unstable due to flaky tests, a common testing-related form of tech debt that I explore in detail in the section “Continuously Testing” on page 245.

假设你已经识别出几个正在拖慢团队的技术债务领域。也许你的 CI 流水线因为不稳定的测试而不稳定——这是一种常见的与测试相关的技术债务，我在第 245 页“持续测试”一节详细探讨过。

Or maybe you're dealing with outdated third-party libraries that are blocking new features, or a core module that hasn't been refactored in years and now takes hours to onboard new team members.

又或者你在处理过时的第三方库，它们挡住了新功能；或者一个多年未重构的核心模块，现在让新团队成员上手要花好几个小时。

These issues are clear signs of tech debt, and they highlight the kind of day-to-day friction that creeps into development if left unchecked. You want to address them.

这些问题是技术债务的明确信号，它们凸显了那种如果放任不管就会悄悄爬进开发的日常摩擦。你想解决它们。

There are two ways to sell it to stakeholders.

向干系人推销有两种方式。

The first is tactical and immediate: speak their language. Connect tech debt efforts to what they care most about: faster delivery, reduced risk, improved relia-bility. Explain how resolving flaky tests or refactoring brittle code can improve release stability, reduce hotfixes, and create space for faster feature work, fewer production issues, and happier customers. Start small. Pick something easy to fix that has a visible impact. Then measure and share the result: how much time was saved, how frustration went down, how the team feels more confident. Bring it up in retros, in sprint reviews, in casual updates. Let them see the improvement.

第一种是战术性的、即时的：说他们的语言。把技术债务工作与他们最关心的东西联系起来：更快的交付、更低的风险、更好的可靠性。解释修复不稳定测试或重构脆弱代码如何能提升发布稳定性、减少热修复、并为更快的功能开发、更少的生产问题、更满意的客户创造空间。从小处开始。挑一个容易修、影响可见的东西。然后衡量并分享结果：省了多少时间、挫败感降了多少、团队信心如何提升。在回顾会、迭代评审、日常同步中把它提出来。让他们看到改进。

The second way is strategic and long term: play the long game. Build trust continuously. Don't wait until you need something to engage with stakeholders.

第二种方式是战略性的、长期的：打长期战。持续建立信任。不要等到你需要什么时才去和干系人互动。

— PDF p.269 —

Keep them in the loop. Show steady progress. Invite feedback. Make them part of the journey. When you've built that relationship, getting buy-in is no longer a battle.

让他们知情。展示稳步的进展。邀请反馈。让他们成为旅程的一部分。一旦你建立了那种关系，获得支持就不再是一场战斗。

To navigate these conversations, use the three Rs of the stakeholder align-ment framework:

要驾驭这些对话，使用干系人对齐框架的三个 R：

Reframe重新框定

Translate tech debt into business value. Don't describe it as cleanup. Show how it leads to faster delivery, fewer incidents, and smoother onboarding.

把技术债务翻译成业务价值。不要把它描述成“清理”。展示它如何带来更快的交付、更少的故障、更顺畅的入职。

Relate建立关联

Link the impact of tech debt to stakeholder pain points. Maybe it's been blocking a feature or increasing the time spent on support. Make it relevant to their goals.

把技术债务的影响与干系人的痛点联系起来。也许它一直在挡住某个功能，或增加了花在支持上的时间。让它与他们的目标相关。

Reinforce持续强化

Regularly share outcomes and updates. Build a track record of small wins to create confidence and momentum for larger investments.

定期分享成果和进展。用一连串小胜建立记录，为更大的投入创造信心和势头。

I rarely got pushback from stakeholders as a tech lead because I put effort into building trust over time. I didn't talk to them only when I needed some-thing; I kept them in the loop consistently, not just when things went wrong. I shared progress regularly, asked for their feedback, and included them in key moments. Over time, that steady communication built a foundation of trust that paid off when we needed space to focus on tech debt or internal improvements.

作为技术负责人，我很少从干系人那里遇到抵制，因为我长期投入于建立信任。我不是只在需要什么时才找他们；我持续让他们知情，而不只是在出问题时。我定期分享进展、征求他们的反馈、让他们参与关键时刻。随着时间推移，那种稳定的沟通建立了信任的基础，当我们需要空间聚焦技术债务或内部改进时，这份信任就兑现了。

So when my team needed to tackle tech debt, there was not much debate: “We need to add this to the sprint. This requires us to remove this feature from the sprint, but we've already reviewed the timeline, and it won't have any negative impact.” The response was simple and confident: “If you say it's needed, it's needed. Sounds good. I trust you.”

所以当我的团队需要处理技术债务时，没什么可争论的：“我们需要把这个加进迭代。这需要我们从迭代里拿掉那个功能，但我们已经看过时间线，不会有任何负面影响。”回答简单而自信：“如果你说需要，那就需要。听起来不错。我信你。”

The point of this story is to show you that there's a different approach, one where you collaborate with stakeholders instead of constantly pushing against them.

这个故事的要点是向你展示：存在另一种方式——你与干系人协作，而不是不断地顶着他们干。

This kind of working relationship doesn't happen overnight. It requires openness on both sides, consistent effort, and a bit of good faith. But when you build that foundation, it changes everything. Conversations become easier. Buy-in becomes natural.

这种工作关系不是一夜之间建立的。它需要双方的开放、持续的努力、以及一点善意。但当你建好那个基础，它会改变一切。对话变得更容易。获得支持变得自然而然。

— PDF p.270 —

Dealing with Incidents处理故障事件

Even in the best-engineered systems, failures happen. Servers crash. Deploys misfire. APIs time out. A third-party system breaks unexpectedly. These moments are stressful, but they're also inevitable.

即使在工程做得最好的系统里，故障也会发生。服务器崩溃。部署出错。API 超时。第三方系统意外挂掉。这些时刻让人压力山大，但它们也不可避免。

There is nothing you can do to prevent all incidents, but there is a lot you can do to ensure your team is prepared to respond well when they happen.

你无法做任何事来阻止所有故障发生，但你可以做很多事来确保你的团队在故障发生时做好了妥善响应的准备。

Actually, how your team responds to an incident is a direct reflection of your engineering culture.

实际上，你的团队如何响应一次故障，是对你工程文化的直接反映。

Build a culture of readiness and learning建立随时待命、持续学习的文化

Incident response isn't just reactive; it's proactive.

故障响应不只是被动的；它是主动的。

Start by normalizing incidents as a natural part of running software. Instead of being surprised or panicking when one happens, build a clear incident han-dling process that helps you stay in control. The following list will help you set up a solid, team-friendly response process:

先把故障正常化，把它当作运行软件的自然一部分。不要在故障发生时惊讶或恐慌，而是建立一个清晰的故障处理流程，帮你保持掌控。下面这份清单会帮你建立一个扎实的、对团队友好的响应流程：

  • Integrate company processes: Many companies already have incident management processes at the organizational level. Make sure your team's process integrates with them. For example, some companies require different levels of stakeholder involvement depending on the incident's severity. Don't reinvent the wheel; adapt it and make sure your team knows it.融入公司流程：很多公司在组织层面已有故障管理流程。确保你团队的流程与它们集成。例如，有些公司要求根据故障严重程度让不同层级的干系人参与。不要重造轮子；改造它，并确保你的团队知道它。
  • Define severity levels and classifications: Not all incidents are created equal. Your login process breaking for all users is very different from it failing only for browser versions outside of your supported set. The number of users impacted, the risk of business loss: these factors matter. Your incident process should adapt based on severity: who gets involved, which communication channels are triggered, and how involved you need to be as a tech lead.定义严重级别和分类：不是所有故障都生而平等。你的登录流程对所有用户挂掉，与它只对你支持范围之外的浏览器版本失效，是非常不同的。受影响的用户数、业务损失的风险：这些因素都重要。你的故障流程应根据严重程度调整：谁参与、触发哪些沟通渠道、以及你作为技术负责人需要介入多深。
  • Make escalation paths obvious: Everyone should know how to escalate an issue and where to find critical information like logs and metrics.让升级路径显而易见：每个人都应该知道如何升级一个问题、以及在哪里找到日志和指标这类关键信息。
  • Invest in observability: Go beyond alerting; make sure your systems are instrumented and your team can actually debug them (more on this in the section “Aim for Fast Feedback” on page 287).投资可观测性：不要只停留在告警；确保你的系统被埋点、你的团队真的能调试它们（详见第 287 页“追求快速反馈”一节）。
— PDF p.271 —
  • Define clear on-call processes: You can't respond quickly to incidents if no one knows who's responsible. That's why you need a clear and reliable on-call process, even for small teams. There should always be someone designated to keep an eye on alerts, investigate issues quickly, and coordinate a response when something breaks. Without this ownership, it's easy for problems to go unnoticed or for everyone to assume someone else is handling it. Most tech teams solve this with an on-call rotation, where responsibility is shared across the team. Tools like PagerDuty or Opsgenie make this process smoother by automatically rotating who's on call, sending alerts, and even escalating if the first person doesn't respond. These tools help ensure no incident goes unacknowledged, whether it happens during working hours or in the middle of the night. More on how to handle after-hours incidents in the section “How to deal with issues outside of working hours” on page 260. But regardless of timing, the on-call process should be clear, fair, and automated.定义清晰的值班流程：如果没人知道谁负责，你就无法快速响应故障。这就是为什么你需要一个清晰、可靠的值班流程，即使对小团队也是如此。应该始终有指定的人盯着告警、快速调查问题、并在出问题时协调响应。没有这种所有权，问题很容易被忽视，或者每个人都以为别人在处理。大多数技术团队用值班轮换来解决这个问题，责任在团队中分担。PagerDuty 或 Opsgenie 这类工具让这个流程更顺畅：自动轮换谁值班、发送告警、甚至在第一个人没响应时升级。这些工具有助于确保没有任何故障未被确认，无论它发生在工作时间还是半夜。关于如何处理下班后的故障，详见第 260 页“如何处理工作时间之外的问题”一节。但无论时间如何，值班流程都应该清晰、公平、自动化。
  • Prepare for things going wrong: Consider running premortems: before major releases, gather your team and ask: “If something goes wrong, what would it be?” This simple question can reveal hidden risks, raise concerns that haven't been voiced, and help you stress-test your rollout plan. You'll often catch potential issues before they turn into real ones. Alongside identifying risks, plan for your rollback path before you need it. It's not enough to hope you won't need one; make sure you can roll back safely and quickly. What's the trigger for deciding to revert? Who owns that decision? How long will it take? What's the impact?为出事做好准备：考虑做事前验尸（premortem）：在重大发布之前，召集团队问：“如果出了问题，会是什么？”这个简单的问题能揭示隐藏的风险、提出尚未被说出的担忧、并帮你压力测试你的发布计划。你常常能在潜在问题变成真问题之前抓住它们。除了识别风险，在你需要回滚路径之前就把它规划好。光希望你不会需要它是不够的；确保你能安全、快速地回滚。决定回滚的触发条件是什么？谁拥有那个决策？要花多久？影响是什么？
  • Prepare for postmortems: Have a simple template ready to make postmortems easy to run and lessons easy to document. (More details to come in the section “What to do post-incident” on page 259.)为复盘做好准备：准备好一个简单的模板，让复盘容易开、教训容易记录。（详见第 259 页“事件处理后该做什么”一节。）
  • Train and practice: Make sure your team and stakeholders are familiar with the incident process. Best way? Run dry runs. Host incident drills, also known as game days, where you simulate real failure scenarios and go through the full response flow.训练并演练：确保你的团队和干系人熟悉故障流程。最好的方式是什么？做空跑。举办故障演练，也叫游戏日（game day），在其中模拟真实故障场景并走完整响应流程。
— PDF p.272 —

Even just one or two a quarter makes a massive difference in prepared-ness. These exercises help everyone stay sharp, ensure responsibilities are clear, and test the actual tools and processes you'll rely on during a real incident. This kind of practice is especially valuable when things are calm. Processes that aren't exercised can quietly go stale, so it's good to take advantage of quieter times to review them. You can also experiment with more advanced resilience practices, like chaos engineering tools (e.g., Chaos Monkey), to intentionally inject failure and test system and team responses.

即使每季度只做一两次，也会让准备程度大不一样。这些练习帮每个人保持敏锐、确保职责清晰、并测试你在真实故障中会依赖的实际工具和流程。这种练习在风平浪静时尤其有价值。不被演练的流程会悄悄过期，所以趁安静的时候复习它们是件好事。你还可以尝试更高级的韧性实践，比如混沌工程工具（例如 Chaos Monkey），故意注入故障并测试系统和团队的响应。

The more familiar and practiced your team is with the process, the less stressful incidents will be, and the more likely you are to turn a crisis into an opportunity for learning.

你的团队对流程越熟悉、演练得越多，故障就越不让人紧张，你也就越有可能把一次危机变成一次学习的机会。

What to do during the incident事件发生期间该做什么

Even with the best preparation, incidents will happen, and how you lead during them matters. When an incident strikes, your role as a tech lead becomes even more crucial.

即使有最好的准备，故障也会发生，而你在故障期间如何领导至关重要。当故障来袭时，你作为技术负责人的角色变得更加关键。

First, make sure people are not losing it. During an incident, your team will look to you to set the tone. If you panic, they will panic. If you stay calm and steady, they will stay calm and steady. So take a breath, stay composed, and help them focus on solving the problem.

首先，确保大家没有失控。在故障期间，团队会看你来定调子。如果你慌，他们就会慌。如果你保持冷静、沉稳，他们就会冷静、沉稳。所以深呼吸，保持镇定，帮他们聚焦于解决问题。

Second, make sure everyone is clear on their role during the incident. Clear roles remove chaos. You should hear things like “I'll check the logs,” “I'll moni-tor alerts,” “I'll coordinate with the PM and customer support.” Most problems under pressure happen when people step on each other's toes or block each other because no one knows who's supposed to do what. Don't let that happen in your team.

第二，确保每个人都清楚自己在故障期间的角色。清晰的角色消除混乱。你应该听到这样的话：“我去查日志”“我盯着告警”“我去和 PM 及客户支持协调”。压力之下出的大多数问题，都发生在人们互相踩脚、或互相挡住的时候——因为没人知道谁该做什么。不要让这种事在你的团队里发生。

Next, regardless of whether you are officially the incident owner or not, you need to protect the developers who are solving the problem. Shield them from stakeholder noise. Very importantly, don't put more pressure on them. Support them. For example, if a senior leader starts pinging the developer for live updates during an incident, step in and offer to provide updates yourself so the team can stay focused on resolving the issue. And if you're not the assigned owner, jump in to help manage stakeholders if you see that the owner is struggling or overwhelmed.

接下来，无论你是不是正式的故障负责人，你都需要保护正在解决问题的开发者。把干系人的噪音挡在外面。非常重要的是，不要给他们施加更多压力。支持他们。例如，如果一位高层领导在故障期间开始不停地催要实时更新，你就介入，由你来提供更新，好让团队能继续聚焦于解决问题。而如果你不是被指定的负责人，当你看到负责人在挣扎或不堪重负时，就跳进去帮他管理干系人。

— PDF p.273 —

Another key part of your role is removing blockers. If the solvers need anything, like access to a certain system or support from another team, you step in. Use your authority and network to speed things up so they can stay focused on fixing the issue.

你角色的另一个关键部分是移除阻塞。如果解决问题的人需要任何东西——比如对某个系统的访问权限或另一个团队的支持——你就介入。用你的职权和人脉把事情推快，好让他们能继续聚焦于修复问题。

Now that we've covered your specific leadership role during an incident, let's shift into the practical side: how to manage the incident process itself:

既然我们已经讲了你在故障期间的具体领导角色，现在转到实操面：如何管理故障流程本身：

  • Assign a clear owner: Every incident needs a coordinator: someone who keeps the response on track by organizing efforts, maintaining communication, and shielding the team from distractions. This person is responsible for sharing updates with the team, stakeholders, external teams like SRE, and users if needed. After the incident, the coordinator also leads the postmortem, assesses business impact, coordinates follow-up work, and ensures documentation is updated. In many teams, this role naturally falls to the on-call engineer, which keeps the process straightforward. Tech leads often feel the urge to step in and take on this responsibility by default. But in practice, the process runs more smoothly when others are empowered to lead, and the tech lead supports them while focusing on broader priorities like business impact and long-term strategy.指派一个清晰的负责人：每次故障都需要一个协调人：一个通过组织力量、保持沟通、并把团队与干扰隔开，让响应走在正轨上的人。这个人负责向团队、干系人、SRE 这类外部团队、以及必要时向用户分享更新。故障之后，协调人还主持复盘、评估业务影响、协调后续工作、并确保文档被更新。在很多团队里，这个角色自然落在值班工程师身上，这让流程很直接。技术负责人常常忍不住默认自己跳出来担起这个责任。但实际上，当被赋权的人来领导、技术负责人在一旁支持并聚焦于业务影响和长期战略等更宽泛的优先事项时，流程运转得更顺畅。
  • Define the issue and assess severity: The first step is helping the owner define the severity of the incident. Before jumping into solution mode, they need clarity on what's actually happening and how serious it is. Sometimes the impact is obvious: your system is down and users are blocked. But other times, like in edge deployments or customer escalations, the scope is less clear. Support them by bringing in the right people: engineers, product managers, support staff, and business stakeholders. Together, collect the facts and answer: What exactly is happening, and how widespread is it? Are users impacted? Is revenue, data, or reputation at risk? If your company has a documented severity framework, this is the time to use it. If not, add it to your post-incident list to define one. Clear thresholds prevent noncritical issues from shortcutting regular delivery processes and being treated as urgent unnecessarily.定义问题并评估严重程度：第一步是帮负责人定义故障的严重程度。在跳进解决方案模式之前，他们需要清楚到底发生了什么、有多严重。有时影响很明显：你的系统挂了，用户被挡住了。但另一些时候——比如边缘部署或客户升级——范围就没那么清楚。通过拉来对的人来支持他们：工程师、产品经理、支持人员、业务干系人。一起收集事实并回答：到底发生了什么、波及多广？用户受影响了吗？收入、数据或声誉有风险吗？如果你的公司有一份成文的严重程度框架，现在就是用它的时候。如果没有，把它加进你的故障后清单去定义一个。清晰的阈值能防止非关键问题抄近路绕过常规交付流程、被不必要地当作紧急事处理。
— PDF p.274 —

Starting with severity ensures the team responds with the right level of urgency and keeps things proportionate, focused, and aligned.

从严重程度入手，确保团队以恰当的紧迫感响应，让事情保持相称、聚焦、对齐。

  • Clearly define solvers: The people actively working to resolve the problem must be explicitly identified. Without clear roles, everyone scrambles and progress slows. Solvers should be protected from stakeholder pressure and distractions. It's also worth emphasizing this: the team's top priority during an incident is to restore service, not to find the root cause. That can come later. Often, a simple revert or a temporary scale-up can stabilize things quickly. Once the system is back in a healthy state, you can take your time identifying what went wrong.明确界定解决者：主动着手解决问题的人必须被明确指认出来。没有清晰的角色，所有人都乱作一团，进展变慢。解决者应被保护起来，不受干系人压力和干扰。这一点也值得强调：故障期间团队的首要任务是恢复服务，而不是找到根因。根因可以以后再来找。通常，一次简单的回滚或临时扩容就能快速稳定局面。一旦系统恢复健康状态，你就可以从容地找出哪里出了问题。
  • Establish a clear communication process: Poor communication can turn a manageable incident into chaos. If there are no regular updates, people get nervous. If solvers are constantly interrupted for status checks, they can't focus. Agree up front how you'll communicate: regular verbal check-ins, updating a shared doc, or quick syncs every few hours. Personally, I prefer quick live check-ins to make sure everyone's aligned. Whatever you pick, stick to it. Resist the urge to start pinging solvers; your role is to act as a shield so they can focus on fixing the issue. Stakeholders need updates, even when there's no major progress yet. If you don't update them, anxiety rises, and they might start distracting the team. Establish early on who communicates with them, how often, and through which channel, whether it's a Slack thread, email updates, or short status meetings. If the incident affects users, you may need to send updates through Statuspage, email notifications, or other public channels. Even when you don't have all the answers yet, sharing early updates helps build trust and shows transparency.建立清晰的沟通流程：糟糕的沟通能把一次可控的故障变成混乱。如果没有定期更新，人会紧张。如果解决者不断被打断问状态，他们就无法聚焦。事先约定你们如何沟通：定期口头同步、更新一个共享文档、或每几小时快速对齐一次。就我个人而言，我更喜欢快速的实时同步来确保大家对齐。无论你选哪种，都坚持下去。抵制住去戳解决者的冲动；你的角色是当一面盾牌，让他们能聚焦于修复问题。干系人需要更新，即使还没有重大进展。如果你不更新他们，焦虑会上升，他们可能开始干扰团队。尽早确定谁与他们沟通、多久一次、通过哪个渠道——无论是一个 Slack 话题串、邮件更新、还是简短的状态会。如果故障影响用户，你可能需要通过 Statuspage、邮件通知或其他公开渠道发送更新。即使你还没有所有答案，分享早期更新也有助于建立信任、展示透明度。
  • Track progress visibly: Log follow-ups clearly. Use Jira, Confluence, your tech debt board, whatever works. Just make sure it's visible and owned.可见地跟踪进度：清晰地记录后续事项。用 Jira、Confluence、你的技术债务看板，什么管用用什么。只要确保它可见、有人负责即可。

With the right leadership and preparation, incidents don't have to be disas-ters; they can be the moments when your team becomes even stronger.

有了正确的领导和准备，故障不必是灾难；它们可以成为让你的团队变得更强大的时刻。

— PDF p.275 —

What to do post-incident事件处理后该做什么

Once the incident is resolved, the real work begins.

一旦故障解决，真正的工作才开始。

First, make sure any official documentation that needs updating is taken care of: business impact reports, incident summaries, customer communications, anything stakeholders need visibility on. This should be the incident owner's responsibility, but as a tech lead, you should make sure it happens.

首先，确保任何需要更新的官方文档都被处理好：业务影响报告、故障摘要、客户沟通、任何干系人需要看到的东西。这本应是故障负责人的职责，但作为技术负责人，你应该确保它发生。

Next, create runbooks for common issues. If something caused an incident, document it. Make it easier for the team to respond faster and better next time. Every incident is a learning opportunity, so treat it like one.

接下来，为常见问题创建运行手册（runbook）。如果某样东西导致了故障，就把它记录下来。让团队下次能更快、更好地响应。每次故障都是一次学习机会，所以这样对待它。

Run a blameless postmortem within 48 hours while the details are still fresh, regardless of how “big” the incident was. Invite everyone who was involved: the main team, supporting teams, and relevant stakeholders.

在 48 小时内开一次无指责的复盘会，趁细节还新鲜，无论故障“大”还是“小”。邀请所有相关的人：主团队、支持团队、以及相关干系人。

Some teams even go a step further and make their incident review meetings open to all engineers in the company. Anyone can join, listen in, and learn. This level of transparency isn't required, but it might be something you want to consider.

有些团队甚至更进一步，把故障评审会对公司所有工程师开放。任何人都可以加入、旁听、学习。这种程度的透明不是必须的，但也许是你想考虑的。

The purpose of a postmortem is to understand what went wrong in the system and identify how to improve it. The key questions to answer are: What happened? Why did it happen? What can we improve? Some of the best improve-ments come from incidents.

复盘的目的是理解系统中哪里出了问题、并识别如何改进它。要回答的关键问题是：发生了什么？为什么发生？我们能改进什么？一些最好的改进正来自故障。

Documentation is a crucial part of turning incidents into learning opportuni-ties. A well-structured postmortem makes it easier for others to learn from the experience and ensures transparency. A good postmortem usually includes the information reflected in Table 8-2.

文档是把故障变成学习机会的关键一环。一份结构良好的复盘让别人更容易从这次经历中学习，并确保透明度。一份好的复盘通常包含表 8-2 所反映的信息。

This structure ensures clarity, transparency, and shared learning across the team and organization.

这种结构确保整个团队和组织内的清晰、透明和共享学习。

Share the documentation widely, and make sure the whole team (and even other teams) can learn from it.

广泛分享文档，确保整个团队（甚至其他团队）都能从中学习。

Make sure to follow up on action items. Assigning tasks isn't enough. Set a clear due date for each one, and check in a few weeks later to make sure follow-ups are completed.

务必跟进行动项。分配任务是不够的。给每一项设定清晰的截止日期，并在几周后回访，确保后续事项被完成。

Add them to the team's regular workflow, whether that's Jira, Trello, or your shared Kanban board, so they stay visible. Make sure they are prioritized alongside other work and given the right level of urgency.

把它们加进团队的常规工作流——无论是 Jira、Trello 还是你们共享的看板——让它们保持可见。确保它们与其他工作一起被排优先级，并被赋予恰当的紧急程度。

Without this kind of accountability, postmortem learnings stay talk instead of action.

没有这种问责，复盘的教训就停留在嘴上，而非行动。

— PDF p.276 —

Postmortems help build a culture where it's safe to talk about problems, and safe to get better, together.

复盘有助于建立一种文化：在这里谈论问题是安全的，一起变得更好也是安全的。

Table 8-2. Postmortem template / 表 8-2. 复盘模板

Postmortem template 复盘模板
Date 日期Date of the postmortem 复盘日期
Author(s) 作者People documenting the postmortem 记录复盘的人
Status 状态Assuming the incident is resolved, here you can add extra details about the status, like “action items in progress” 假设故障已解决，可在此补充状态的额外细节，如“行动项进行中”
Summary 摘要A quick overview of what happened 发生了什么的快速概览
Impact 影响What was affected and how 什么受了影响、影响如何
Priority 优先级The severity classification (e.g., low, medium, high) 严重程度分类（如低、中、高）
Incident coordinator 故障协调人Who was responsible for managing the response 谁负责管理响应
Start time 开始时间When the incident began 故障何时开始
Resolved time 解决时间When the immediate issue was resolved 直接问题何时解决
Closed time 关闭时间When all follow-ups and documentation were completed 所有后续事项和文档何时完成
People involved 参与人员List of everyone involved in the response 参与响应的所有人列表
Incident communication channels 故障沟通渠道Slack channel or comms method used for coordinating the response 用于协调响应的 Slack 频道或沟通方式
Customer communication 客户沟通Whether customers were affected and if communication was needed 是否影响了客户、是否需要沟通
Root cause(s) 根因What triggered the incident 是什么触发了故障
Detection 发现How it was discovered or missed 它是如何被发现或漏掉的
Response 响应What actions were taken 采取了哪些行动
Timeline 时间线Key events and timestamps 关键事件和时间戳
Lessons learned 经验教训What went well, what didn't 哪些做得好、哪些不好
Follow-up actions 后续行动Specific tasks with owners and deadlines 带负责人和截止日期的具体任务

How to deal with issues outside of working hours如何处理工作时间之外的问题

I used to be completely against the idea of on-call support. My mindset was always “We need to build systems that don't require people to be woken up at night.” I thought my team was fully aligned with that too. So when the client suggested introducing an official paid on-call process, I assumed it would be a hard no from us.

我曾经完全反对值班待命这个想法。我的心态一直是“我们需要构建不需要半夜把人叫醒的系统”。我以为我的团队也完全认同这一点。所以当客户建议引入一个官方的带薪值班流程时，我以为我们一定会坚决拒绝。

Surprisingly, some team members were interested. Because the reality is, no matter how good your system is, there are always things that can go wrong outside working hours. And the truth was, we were already covering incidents outside of working hours, just informally, and we weren't getting compensated for it.

令人惊讶的是，有些团队成员有兴趣。因为现实是，无论你的系统多好，总会有东西在工作时间外出问题。而真相是，我们本来就已经在非正式地处理工作时间外的故障，却没有因此拿到任何补偿。

— PDF p.277 —

In the end, we voted as a team. We decided to stick to no official on-call system, but we promised to work even harder to minimize after-hours issues. We also introduced a small reward system: if you had to work at night, you could take time off during the day, one hour for every hour worked. Looking back, I realize now that pushing so hard against on-call might not have been the best move for my team.

最后，我们作为一个团队投票。我们决定坚持不设官方值班制度，但承诺更加努力地减少下班后的问题。我们还引入了一个小小的奖励机制：如果你不得不在晚上工作，你可以在白天补休，工作一小时补休一小时。回头看，我现在意识到，如此强烈地反对值班，对我的团队也许并不是最好的选择。

The reality is that systems will break outside working hours. Some problems can wait until morning or Monday. Others can't. Either way, you need to have a clear conversation with your team and stakeholders about how you'll handle these situations. And most importantly, whatever system you put in place, make sure people are properly compensated for their time and effort.

现实是系统一定会在工作时间外出问题。有些问题可以等到早上或周一。另一些等不了。无论哪种，你都需要和你的团队、干系人就如何处理这些情况进行一次清晰的对话。而最重要的是，无论你建立什么制度，都要确保人们的时间和付出得到恰当的补偿。

I've seen two common models for on-call compensation:

我见过两种常见的值班补偿模式：

Per time按值班时间补偿

You get paid for simply being on call during a rotation window, whether or not anything breaks. I've noticed that this model motivates teams to improve their systems, accumulate less tech debt, and have fewer recurring issues, because there's a better chance of “getting paid to do nothing.”

只要在值班轮换窗口内待命就有报酬，无论有没有东西坏。我注意到这种模式会激励团队改进系统、积累更少的技术债务、出现更少的反复问题，因为“什么都不做也能拿钱”的机会更大。

Per incident按故障次数补偿

You get paid only if you actually have to jump in and fix something. This can sometimes backfire; if people get paid only when things go wrong, there's less incentive to proactively fix root causes or invest in system improvements.

只有当你真的跳进去修东西时才拿到钱。这有时会适得其反；如果人们只有在出事时才拿到钱，主动修复根因或投资于系统改进的动力就更少。

Whatever you choose, sit down with your team and stakeholders. Define clear on-call rotations, responsibilities, and expectations. Document the process, make it visible, and add it to your onboarding checklist and ways of working as a team.

无论你选哪种，都和你的团队、干系人坐下来谈。定义清晰的值班轮换、职责和期待。把流程写成文档、让它可见，并把它加进你的入职清单和团队工作方式里。

A great incident response process is a team effort. It starts with preparation, shows up in how you communicate during a crisis, and continues long after the issue is resolved. When handled well, incidents can actually strengthen your systems, your team, and your trust with stakeholders.

一个好的故障响应流程是团队的共同努力。它始于准备，体现在危机期间你如何沟通，并在问题解决后持续很久。处理得当时，故障实际上可以强化你的系统、你的团队、以及你与干系人的信任。

— PDF p.278 —

Documentation or No Documentation?要不要写文档？

There's always been a long-standing divide among developers when it comes to documentation. Some are firmly against it, while others are fully in favor.

在文档这件事上，开发者之间一直存在长期的分歧。一些人坚决反对，另一些人完全赞成。

As always, the answer is somewhere in the middle, and it depends on what kind of documentation we're actually talking about.

和往常一样，答案在中间的某个地方，而且取决于我们实际在谈的是哪种文档。

The common critique is that documentation goes stale and that the code should be the ultimate source of truth. It's true that some forms of documenta-tion, like implementation notes, can become outdated quickly, and yes, in an ideal world, code would be expressive and clear enough to speak for itself. But let's be honest: how often is the codebase that clean and easy to understand?

常见的批评是：文档会过时，代码才应该是最终的真相来源。确实，某些形式的文档——比如实现笔记——可能很快过时；也确实，在理想世界里，代码应该足够富有表达力、足够清晰，能自己说话。但说实话：代码库那么干净、那么易读的时候有几次？

On top of that, many things simply can't be captured in code. Team pro-cesses, roadmaps, architectural decisions, operational runbooks: these aren't things you can read from a function or a class. These kinds of documents don't exist to explain what the code is doing but to explain why decisions were made and how to work with the system and the team behind it.

除此之外，很多东西根本无法用代码捕捉。团队流程、路线图、架构决策、运维手册：这些不是你能从一个函数或一个类里读出来的东西。这类文档的存在，不是为了解释代码在做什么，而是为了解释为什么做了这些决策、以及如何与这个系统和它背后的团队协作。

I don't think the right question is “Documentation or no documentation?” It's more about how to do documentation effectively. What should be docu-mented, and how do we keep it useful?

我不认为正确的问题是“要不要文档”。更重要的是如何有效地写文档。什么应该被记录下来？我们又如何让它保持有用？

Personally, I lean toward writing things down. As a tech lead, I've seen how valuable even lightweight documentation can be, especially for onboarding new team members, reducing dependencies on specific individuals, aligning the team, and debugging issues that surface months later.

就我个人而言，我倾向于把事情写下来。作为技术负责人，我见过即使是轻量级文档也能多有价值——尤其是在新成员入职、减少对特定个人的依赖、对齐团队、以及调试几个月后才冒出来的问题方面。

Yes, documentation takes effort, and no, it won't always stay perfectly in sync with reality. But even slightly outdated docs can still be useful; they give you something to update, challenge, or validate. That's far better than having no starting point at all.

是的，写文档要花精力；不，它不会永远和现实完美同步。但即使稍微过时的文档仍然有用；它们给你一个可以去更新、去质疑、去验证的东西。这比完全没有起点要好得多。

The value of documentation文档的价值

Documentation plays a powerful role across many aspects of your work as a tech lead. It becomes critical when tracking architecture changes (check out the section “Visualizing a System Architecture” on page 226), managing tech debt (check out the section “Managing Technical Debt” on page 249, and learn-ing from incidents (check out the section “What to do post-incident” on page 259). Without clear records of why decisions were made or what trade-offs were accepted, teams fall into confusion, repeat mistakes, or rebuild solutions to prob-lems they already solved.

文档在你作为技术负责人工作的很多方面都扮演着强有力的角色。在跟踪架构变更（见第 226 页“可视化系统架构”一节）、管理技术债务（见第 249 页“管理技术债务”一节）、以及从故障中学习（见第 259 页“事件处理后该做什么”一节）时，它变得至关重要。没有关于为什么做了这些决策、接受了哪些取舍的清晰记录，团队就会陷入混乱、重复犯错、或为已经解决过的问题重新造轮子。

— PDF p.279 —

The biggest value of documentation is alignment, with your team, stakehold-ers, and even your future self. It keeps reasoning visible and decisions anchored, and it gives everyone a shared reference point when things drift: “This is what we agreed on; what changed?”

文档最大的价值是对齐——与你的团队、干系人、甚至未来的你自己对齐。它让推理过程可见、让决策有锚点，并在事情漂移时给所有人一个共享的参照点：“这是我们当时同意的；什么变了？”

A great example is documenting your ways of working. These are rarely written down, because everyone assumes: “We know how we do things; we do them every day.” But that might backfire.

一个很好的例子是把你的工作方式写成文档。这些很少被写下来，因为每个人都假设：“我们知道自己怎么做事；我们每天都在做。”但这可能会适得其反。

I once coached a tech lead who was frustrated by shifting priorities. The CTO kept assigning engineers urgent tasks directly, bypassing the team's sprint planning. “She should follow our process,” he said.

我曾辅导过一位技术负责人，他对不断变化的优先级感到沮丧。CTO 不断直接给工程师派紧急任务，绕过了团队的迭代规划。“她应该遵守我们的流程，”他说。

So I asked, “How would the CTO even know your process? Have you walked her through it? Is it written down anywhere?” He paused: “No… I guess I just assumed she knew.”

于是我问：“CTO 怎么会知道你的流程？你带她走过一遍吗？它写在什么地方了吗？”他顿了一下：“没有……我猜我只是假设她知道。”

So he wrote a short, high-level summary of how work enters the backlog, how it's refined, and how prioritization is handled. Then he shared it in the team's workspace and tagged the relevant managers, including the CTO.

于是他写了一份简短的高层摘要：工作如何进入待办列表、如何被细化、以及如何排优先级。然后他把它分享在团队的工作区里，并 @ 了相关的经理们，包括 CTO。

Two days later, the PM messaged him: “I've added a task from the CTO into the backlog for the team to evaluate. We can discuss in refinement.” No more random interruptions. The process held.

两天后，PM 给他发消息：“我已经把 CTO 的一个任务加进待办列表，让团队评估。我们可以在细化会上讨论。”再也没有随机的打断了。流程撑住了。

This example highlights more than just a documentation gap, but the take-away is simple: sometimes, all it takes is writing things down and making them visible.

这个例子凸显的不只是一个文档空白，但要点很简单：有时候，所需要做的只是把事情写下来、让它们可见。

Also, documenting your ways of working can be incredibly valuable for onboarding. New joiners often struggle with unspoken norms or informal pro-cesses. Having these written down—how planning works, how priorities are set, what “done” means—gives them something concrete to refer to.

另外，把你的工作方式写成文档，对新人入职极其有价值。新加入的人常常在不成文的规范或非正式流程中挣扎。把这些写下来——规划怎么运作、优先级怎么定、“完成”意味着什么——就给了他们具体的可参照之物。

But it's not just new joiners who benefit. Even experienced team mem-bers feel the impact when key knowledge is missing. Especially when systems break—and they will—good documentation can save your team hours of confu-sion and stress.

但受益的不只是新人。即使是有经验的团队成员，在关键知识缺失时也会感受到影响。尤其是当系统坏掉时——而它们一定会坏——好的文档能帮你的团队省下数小时的困惑和压力。

One client shared this story with me: her team was working with a legacy system that had become a major source of friction. Every time something broke, it triggered a firefight: hours lost digging through old tickets, chasing down people who'd once worked on the system, and trying to reverse-engineer what the code was supposed to do. Even small incidents caused big delays.

一位客户跟我分享过这个故事：她的团队在处理一个遗留系统，它已经成为摩擦的主要来源。每次出问题，都会触发一场救火：花数小时翻旧工单、追找曾经在这个系统上工作过的人、并试图反推代码本该做什么。即使小故障也造成大延迟。

So she introduced a lightweight habit: any time someone figured something out about how the system worked, like how services interacted, how to restart a flaky job, or what a mysterious config did, they wrote it down in a shared runbook—not overly detailed, just enough for someone else to pick it up later.

于是她引入了一个轻量习惯：每当有人弄明白了系统如何工作的某件事——比如服务之间如何交互、如何重启一个不稳定的任务、或某个神秘配置是干什么的——就把它写进一份共享的运行手册里——不要过于详细，只够别人以后能接着用就行。

— PDF p.280 —

Over time, that runbook became one of the team's most valuable assets. During one major incident, the team even used the runbook in real time to guide their mitigation steps.

随着时间推移，那份运行手册成了团队最有价值的资产之一。在一次重大故障中，团队甚至实时用那份运行手册来指导他们的缓解步骤。

It was a great reminder that documentation doesn't need to be big or formal to make a big impact. It can be as simple as writing things down as you go.

这很好地提醒了我们：文档不必很大、很正式，才能产生大影响。它可以简单到就是一边做一边把事情写下来。

The great news is that these days, the documentation process is way easier because you have better tools. Screen recording tools like Loom, Scribe, or Tango can capture workflows in seconds. AI-assisted notes can summarize your actions and generate documentation as you work. Lightweight templates for runbooks, onboarding guides, and decision logs make it faster to create useful content. And if you update documentation alongside your pull requests and technical changes, it becomes a natural part of development rather than a separate “documentation day” months later.

好消息是，如今写文档的过程容易多了，因为你有更好的工具。像 Loom、Scribe、Tango 这样的屏幕录制工具可以在几秒钟内捕获工作流。AI 辅助笔记可以总结你的动作、在你工作时生成文档。运行手册、入职指南和决策日志的轻量模板让创建有用内容更快。而如果你在提交 pull request 和技术变更的同时更新文档，它就成了开发的自然一部分，而不是几个月后单独拿出来的一个“文档日”。

Of course, there's a risk with these tools too. While they make it easier to generate documentation, they can also lead to disengagement, such as auto-generated docs that no one reads, questions, or updates. To avoid this trap, some-one on the team still needs to take ownership: reviewing content, validating its usefulness, and making sure it stays relevant and integrated into your day-to-day work.

当然，这些工具也有风险。虽然它们让生成文档更容易，但它们也可能导致疏离——比如没人读、没人问、没人更新的自动生成文档。要避开这个陷阱，团队里仍然需要有人担起责任：评审内容、验证它的用处、并确保它保持相关、并融入你的日常工作。

What to document该写什么文档

Here are some things worth documenting and keeping up-to-date as part of your team's day-to-day work:

下面是一些值得作为团队日常工作的一部分记录下来并保持更新的东西：

  • Architecture: Document the current state, desired state, stages of changes, and decisions made along the way (more on this in the section “Architectural Strategies and Implementation” on page 221).架构：记录现状、期望状态、变更阶段、以及一路走来所做的决策（详见第 221 页“架构策略与实施”一节）。
  • Key decisions: Why they were made and what alternatives were considered. This applies not just to architecture but also to product and team processes (more on this in the section “Track Technical Decisions—Architecture Decision Records” on page 281).关键决策：为什么做了这些决策、考虑过哪些备选。这不仅适用于架构，也适用于产品和团队流程（详见第 281 页“跟踪技术决策——架构决策记录”一节）。
  • Incident postmortems and learnings: Capturing what happened, why it happened, and how to prevent it in the future (more on this in the section “Dealing with Incidents” on page 254).故障复盘和教训：记录发生了什么、为什么发生、以及未来如何预防（详见第 254 页“处理故障事件”一节）。
  • Strategies: Examples include your testing strategies, your path to production (more on this in the section “Defining Your Path to Production” on page 239), objectives and key results (OKRs), and the contracts and agreements between your team and other teams or systems.策略：例如你的测试策略、你的上线路径（详见第 239 页“定义你的上线路径”一节）、目标与关键结果（OKR）、以及你团队与其他团队或系统之间的契约和协议。
  • Team processes: Onboarding guides, ways of working, and anything that helps new and existing team members move faster and stay aligned.团队流程：入职指南、工作方式、以及任何帮新老成员走得更快、保持对齐的东西。
  • Infrastructure: If you're using infrastructure-as-code tools like Terraform, your infrastructure can become self-documenting to some degree.基础设施：如果你在用像 Terraform 这样的基础设施即代码工具，你的基础设施在某种程度上可以变成自文档化的。
— PDF p.281 —

The goal is to document the parts of your system, culture, and processes that help your team move quickly and stay aligned, focusing on what's most useful and relevant to your daily work.

目标是记录你系统、文化和流程中那些帮团队快速前进、保持对齐的部分，聚焦于对你日常工作最有用、最相关的东西。

How to keep documentation alive如何让文档保持鲜活

As mentioned before, the biggest issue with documentation is keeping it updated and relevant. There are a couple of strategies that can help you do that.

如前所述，文档最大的问题是保持它更新、相关。有几个策略可以帮你做到。

Make updating relevant documentation part of the “definition of done” for work items. This way, changes in architecture, processes, or systems are reflected immediately.

把更新相关文档作为工作项“完成定义”的一部分。这样，架构、流程或系统的变更就会立刻被反映出来。

Assign a rotating “doc champion” role within your team to periodically review and flag stale documents. Fresh eyes help catch things that otherwise get forgotten.

在团队内指派一个轮换的“文档代言人”角色，定期审查并标出过时的文档。新鲜的眼光有助于抓住那些否则会被遗忘的东西。

Include documentation reviews as part of your retrospectives or team health checks. If something important changed recently, there's probably a document that needs updating too.

把文档评审作为你的回顾会或团队健康检查的一部分。如果最近有重要的东西变了，大概也有一份文档需要更新。

Continuously delete or archive old, misleading, or irrelevant documentation. I have to say this is one of the most satisfying parts of the role: the ability to just go and delete something that's no longer useful. Honestly, it's better than creat-ing documentation. I know it can feel scary to delete things, so here's a strategy I use: archive before you delete. Move the document somewhere inaccessible but retrievable. See if anyone notices, complains, or needs it. If after a while, no one asks for it, you can confidently delete it.

持续删除或归档旧的、误导性的、或不相关的文档。我得说这是这个角色最让人满足的部分之一：能直接去删掉一个不再有用的东西。老实说，这比创建文档还爽。我知道删东西可能让人害怕，所以这里有一个我用的策略：删之前先归档。把文档移到一个不可访问但可找回的地方。看看有没有人注意到、抱怨、或需要它。如果过了一阵子没人要它，你就可以放心地删了。

— PDF p.282 —

Another approach I've used is simply removing access; if someone actually needs it, they'll request it. That becomes a great signal that the document is still in use. You can even take it one step further; when someone does ask for access, start a quick conversation: “What do you use it for?” It might turn out they need something more current or that they were referencing it out of habit, not usefulness. Worst-case scenario, if you do delete it, but it turns out you need it, you'll rebuild it, this time actually relevant and updated.

我用过的另一个方法是直接移除访问权限；如果有人真的需要它，他们会来申请。这就成了一个很好的信号，说明这份文档还在被使用。你甚至可以再进一步：当有人来申请访问时，开启一段简短对话：“你用它做什么？”结果可能是他们需要更新的东西，或者他们只是出于习惯、而非有用性在引用它。最坏的情况是，你真把它删了，结果又需要它，那你就重建一份——这一次它真正相关、真正更新。

If keeping your documentation alive isn't part of your team's routine, it will rot, no matter how beautifully it started.

如果让文档保持鲜活不是你团队日常的一部分，它就会腐烂——无论它一开始写得多漂亮。

Documentation needs to be useful. Document for people, not for process. Make it easy, make it actionable, and make it part of how your team works every day.

文档需要有用。为人写文档，而不是为流程写文档。让它容易读、可执行，并让它成为你团队每天工作方式的一部分。

Key Takeaway本章要点

Great technical leadership means guiding architecture, deployment, and every-day decisions in ways that help your team move fast and build with confidence.

卓越的技术领导力，意味着以帮助团队快速前进、满怀信心构建的方式，去引导架构、部署和日常决策。

Throughout this chapter, we looked at the real, practical responsibilities that shape a healthy engineering culture: evolving architecture, improving delivery pipelines, managing tech debt, handling incidents, and making documentation useful.

在本章中，我们看了塑造健康工程文化的那些真实、实操的责任：演进架构、改进交付流水线、管理技术债务、处理故障事件、以及让文档变得有用。

All of these are part of the same goal: making intentional technical choices that support your team and product over time.

所有这些都服务于同一个目标：做出有意识的技术选择，长期支持你的团队和产品。

Technical work is never separate from people work.

技术工作永远与“人”的工作不可分割。
